## Preface.

I am presenting the public here with a collection of biographies of such people who made it their life’s business to act against philosophy and sound reason, and yet imagined themselves to be great philosophers in the process; or rather, those who placed the very essence of philosophy in this nonsense. I call them <term>monsters</term> <note>Original: *Unholden*. While it often means "fiends" or "monsters" in a mythological sense, Adelung uses it here to describe those who are "un-hold" to reason—intellectual deviants who pervert the natural order of logic.</note>, because I know of no more fitting word to express the general nature of the various <term>fools</term> <note>Original: *Thoren*. A term frequently used by Enlightenment writers to categorize individuals who lacked critical judgment or were easily swayed by superstition.</note> of this kind

## Preface.

expressed it better than this one. I draw these examples primarily from the <term>learned class</term> <note>Original: *gelehrten Classe*. Adelung focuses on scholars and academics because their departure from reason is more "striking" given that their education should have protected them from such delusions.</note>, because the contrast here is most striking, and the sciences ought to protect anyone who is not entirely insane from such excesses.

As philosophy, or rather <term>sound reason</term> <note>Original: *gesunde Vernunft*. A cornerstone of Enlightenment thought, this refers to the natural human capacity for objective, logical judgment, which Adelung believes "takes revenge" on those who ignore it by leading them into chaotic lives.</note>, tends to take immediate revenge on those who work directly against it, their lives are also commonly a series of various shifting fates. This variety can make their stories entertaining even for the idle man who reads merely for pleasure. 

I have therefore believed that such a collection in our day—where reading has become such an essential need—would provide a worthwhile alternative to novels, travelogues, and other contemporary books of this type. I have sought to make these accounts as detailed as the <term>resources</term> <note>Original: *Hülfsmittel*. # Preface

I only regret that reliable, detailed <term>accounts</term> <note>Original: *Nachrichten*. In this period, the term refers to documented reports, news, or biographical facts.</note> of such people are so rarely to be found. Even if they cause a great stir during their own lifetime, the true <term>scholar</term> <note>Original: *Gelehrte*. Many spend their lives wandering <note>Original: *in der Irre*. This carries a double meaning in German: both wandering physically from place to place and wandering mentally in a state of error or delusion.</note>, making it very difficult for their future biographer to gather the necessary information from so many different provinces and countries.

This reflects the 18th-century literary ideal of *Prodesse et Delectare* (to be useful and to please).</note>—and that they all lacked sufficient interest. # Preface

...to collect the necessary <term>accounts</term> <note>Original: *Nachrichten*. This refers to factual reports, documentation, or biographical data.</note> myself, and to supplement the existing <term>biographies</term> <note>Original: *Lebensbeschreibungen*.</note> from them. Just how laborious this often was can best be appreciated by anyone who undertakes a similar task themselves. In this way, that which I had intended merely as a form of light entertainment after more serious labors became, for me, one of my most serious occupations.

However, to make this work useful to the <term>literary scholar</term> <note>Original: *Litterator*. In the 18th century, this referred to a man of letters or a scholar specializing in the history of literature and books.</note> as well, I have not only devoted every possible diligence to the literary portion of these lives, but I have also precisely cited my <term>sources</term> <note>Original: *Quellen*.</note> in every instance—not just in general terms, but for every significant individual detail.

The reason why I have categorized this or that man among the <term>philosophical monsters</term> <note>Original: *philosophischen Unholden*. Adelung uses this colorful term to describe intellectual eccentrics, charlatans, or thinkers whose ideas he considered distorted or "monstrous" by the standards of Enlightenment reason.</note> has been stated in each case where it was necessary; therefore, I need not explain myself further on the matter here.

### Preface

Should this work find **approval** <note>Original: *Beyfall*. This refers to the favorable reception or critical acclaim of the reading public.</note>, it may yet be continued for a long time; for the **realm of folly** is larger than the **realm of wisdom**. Perhaps this **collection** <note>Original: *Sammlung*. Adelung views his work as a curated repository of historical case studies.</note> may become even more remarkable in the future, as I have hope of receiving hitherto entirely unknown <term>accounts</term> <note>Original: *Nachrichten*. In the 18th century, this meant factual reports, news, or documented evidence.</note> regarding several more recent <term>fools</term> <note>Original: *Thoren*. Adelung uses this term not just for the "mad," but for intellectual eccentrics, charlatans, and those who deviated from Enlightenment reason.</note> of this kind.

Berlin, September 25, 1785.

### 1. Bartholomew Cocles.

To apply such accidental circumstances as the features of the face and the lines of the hands or other parts of the body to determine a person's character and even their future destiny is such a misuse of common sense—or rather, such a total lack of it—that the arts built upon these ideas could only find success in very crude and uneducated ages, or among entirely sensory and unenlightened people. And yet, how often have they succeeded? And how often do they succeed even now? To be sure, **physiognomy** <term>physiognomy</term> <note>The practice of assessing a person's character or personality from their outer appearance, particularly the face.</note> has a bit more evidence in its favor than **chiromancy** <term>chiromancy</term> <note>Palmistry; the practice of fortune-telling through the study of the palm.</note> and other similar **pseudo-sciences** <note>Original: *Afterkünste*. Literally "false arts" or "sham-sciences," a derogatory term used by Enlightenment authors to dismiss superstitious practices.</note>, because dominant inclinations very often impart their own character to the facial features, and perhaps also because the structure of the head and its...

I have borrowed this article for the most part from Jovius's *Eulogies of Men Distinguished in Letters* <note>Original Latin: *Elogiis virorum litteris illustr.* A famous biographical work by Paolo Giovio (1483–1552).</note> and Fantuzzi’s *Bolognese Writers* <note>Original: *Scrittori Bolognesi*. Giovanni Fantuzzi (1718–1799) was an Italian historian and biographer.</note>. Other writers, such as Eloy in the *Dictionary of Medicine* <note>Original French: *Dictionn. de la Médecine*.</note> and Carrere in the *Library of Medicine* <note>Original French: *Biblioth. de la Médecine*.</note> mention him only very briefly.

# 1. Bartholomew Cocles.

That his learning must have been of no significance is clear from the fact that he could find pleasure in such meager arts <note>Original: *armseligen Künsten*. The author refers to the "pseudo-sciences" of palmistry and face-reading mentioned on the previous page.</note> and pursued them more than medical science; just as he owes to them alone the little memory of him that still remains. Nevertheless, he must have possessed some grammatical knowledge, because in 1503—the year before his death—he was commissioned by the authorities to teach four "shamefaced poor" <note>Original: *poveri vergognosi*. A historical term for impoverished people of formerly high social standing who were too ashamed to beg for alms.</note> children in his quarter for free.

He caused far more of a stir through **physiognomy** <note>The practice of judging a person's character or fortune from their facial features.</note> and **chiromancy** <note>Palmistry or hand-reading.</note>, arts which had only recently been brought into repute by a certain Antiochus <note>Likely referring to Antiochus Tibertus (c. 1465–1499), a famous contemporary diviner in Italy.</note>. Of this Antiochus, nothing more is known to me, although he is also said to have written on physiognomy and chiromancy. By means of these, Cocles hoped to outstrip the astrologers, whose equally groundless art was one of the **fashionable diseases** of this and the following century. Furthermore, he was not only a great dreamer who dreamed of the fates of others in advance, but also a skilled **interpreter of dreams**. He succeeded in this beyond his expectations, even earning the respect of the great metaphysician and scholastic philosopher, Alessandro Achillini <note>Alessandro Achillini (1463–1512) was a renowned professor of medicine and philosophy at Bologna, known as the "Second Aristotle."</note>, who provided a learned preface to Cocles’ *The Resurrection of Palmistry and Physiognomy* <note>Original Latin title: *Anastasi Chiromantiae ac Physionomiae*. The word "Anastasi" is a Latinization of the Greek word for resurrection.</note>. In this preface, Achillini most earnestly recommended both arts, preferring them far above astrology, and through

# 1. Bartholomew Cocles.

...his reputation sanctioned, as it were, the already prevailing folly. It is not to be wondered at that some predictions—fulfilled by chance or guessed through trickery—blind the great masses, who think no further than what they see. But that a philosopher as great as Achillini was by reputation—being called nothing less than the "second Aristotle"—was capable of such weakness is truly sad, and belongs to the vexing chronicle of the human intellect. For the sake of his honor, one might be inclined to believe that either friendship or self-interest played the largest part in his recommendation of Cocles; however, this suspicion vanishes as soon as one considers that Achillini did not stop at merely recommending Cocles, but degraded himself and his philosophy so far that he himself acted as a teacher of both arts.

He attributed the last work to Cocles. # I. Bartholomew Cocles.

...through his own and Achillini’s charlatanry <note>The original German *Marktschreyerey* suggests the loud, boastful self-promotion typical of street vendors or quacks.</note> he gained such a reputation that not only private individuals but even princes and lords rushed to him to have their future destinies foretold. Among the latter, Galeazzo Sforza—the brother of the Lord of Pesaro—is particularly mentioned; he held Cocles in very high esteem and sought his prophecies. 

Among his learned patrons, aside from Achillini, Paolo Giovio <note>Latin: Paulus Jovius</note> is one of the best known. In his *Eulogies of Men Illustrious in Letters* <note>Original: *Elogiis virorum litteris illustrium*</note>, he speaks of Cocles with great respect and complete confidence in the truth of his art. He claims to have seen a manuscript in Cocles’s own hand in which all the persons were listed to whom he had predicted a violent death. According to Giovio, after Cocles’s death, this list was compared with the actual events and everything was found to be perfectly accurate. # I. Bartholomew Cocles.

As Jovius relates, he had predicted to Ermete Bentivoglio, a son of Giovanni <note>Giovanni II Bentivoglio, the ruler of Bologna until 1506.</note>, that he would be driven from his fatherland and killed in a skirmish. When the murderer was later questioned about the motive for this deed, he could provide no other reason than that Cocles had prophesied to him, from the lines of his hand, that Capponi would shortly commit a murder; therefore, he had felt a calling within himself to make this prophecy come true. Whoever knows how many millennia of fortunate inventions and continuous observations were required before the human spirit perceived in these shimmering little points what they truly are—namely, enormous celestial bodies distributed through an infinite space, moving in orderly circles traced for them by the Creator of the world—will gladly forgive the unrefined man, stripped of all higher knowledge, if he took this luminous host to be either an assembly of the gods, or the noblest of departed souls, or heavenly strokes of a pen containing the destinies of every individual man, or whatever else he might have imagined. It is said that he was appointed Professor of Mathematics and Astronomy at Bologna by the Emperor; others make him a professor in Paris. Perhaps both are right, as it was not uncommon at that time for scholars to travel for the sake of their science and stay for a time at one university and then another. He must also have lived in Padua, because Ezelinus <note>Ezzelino III da Romano (1194–1259), a powerful and notorious Ghibelline leader in Northern Italy.</note>, the Lord of Padua, kept him with him for a time and often had his fortune told by him. Even the Emperor himself, who undertook nothing without first consulting the stars for advice, is said to have kept him at his court with a large salary. The author of the *Ancient and Modern Glories of the City of Forlì* <note>original: "Lustri antichi e moderni della Citta di Forli"</note>, whom Mazzuchelli cites, calls this Emperor Henry. However, since no Emperor of this name lived in this century, Mazzuchelli suspects that one must read "Frederick II" instead. ## 2. Guido Bonatti.

...then Bonatti must have come to his fame very young, which is hardly probable; otherwise, he must have been born earlier than 1230. Bonatti stayed for the longest time with Count Guido Montefeltro, Lord of Forlì, a famous man of war who for that reason was also called the "second Ulysses," but who never undertook a single campaign without first having the stars consulted by Bonatti. Filippo Villani, who lived a century later, has preserved in his *Lives of Illustrious Florentines* <note>original: "Vite de' Vomini illustri Fiorentini"</note> one of the ways in which this trickster <note>The author uses the German word "Gaukler," which translates to "juggler" or "conjurer," implying a skeptical view of Bonatti’s methods as mere performance or deception.</note> went to work. 

Whenever the Count planned a raid, Bonatti would always climb the bell tower of Saint Mercurialis <note>The Abbey of San Mercuriale, a famous Romanesque church in Forlì.</note> to observe the stars (perhaps only to see if the area was safe, for the author does not say whether it happened by day or by night). At the first stroke of the bell, which the interpreter of signs <term>Zeichendeuter: a person who interprets omens or celestial signs, here referring to the astrologer.</term> gave, the Count armed himself with his men; at the second, they mounted their horses; and at the third, they rode out through the gate, and for the most part, they returned home victorious. 

The same author assures us that Bonatti—and, as he wisely adds, not through magical but through astrological art—had a copper statue cast, which represented an armored man on horseback and possessed the gift of prophecy. This was said to be the cause of many of the brave deeds of the Count of Montefeltro, especially in the conquest of the territory of Romagna and the subjugation...

One of the most important instances in which he is said to have predicted future events is the following; at least, it has been recorded as quite remarkable by most writers. Pope Martin IV besieged the city of Forlì, and his troops believed they already had it in their possession. Bonatti, assured of something different from the stars, determined the hour when the Count should make a secret sortie and promised him victory, which indeed followed successfully. 

But who does not see that this could have occurred even without any astrological art, especially when the courage of the besieged was inflamed by their confidence in the fortune-teller’s <term>Wahrsager: a soothsayer or diviner; here used skeptically to describe the astrologer’s influence.</term> skill? Such ruses to make common soldiers brave were already common among the most ancient peoples. In the 20th Canto <note>original: "20sten Ges."</note> of the *Inferno*, Dante calls upon the reader to look at Bonatti and Asdente, a poor shoemaker <note>The original German "Schuflicker" implies a cobbler or one who repairs old shoes.</note> from Parma, who likewise meddled in astrology.

[...First: to] contradict the judgments made against the stars. <note>original: "Astrorum Judiciis contradicere." This refers to the twelve signs of the Zodiac.</note> Third: On the seven planets, and what happens to one because of another, and those things which pertain to the eighth sphere. <note>original: "Tertio de septem Planetis, et quid accidat uni eorum ab altero, et de his quae ad octavam Sphaeram spectant." In medieval cosmology, the "eighth sphere" was the firmament containing the fixed stars, located beyond the spheres of the seven known planets.</note> Fourth: I shall touch upon certain conjunctions. <note>original: "Quarto innuam de quibusdam Conjunctionibus."</note> Fifth: On certain considerations that occur in judgments. <note>original: "Quinto de quibusdam considerationibus quae cadunt in Judiciis."</note> Sixth: I shall set forth a portion of the judgments. <note>original: "Sexto ponam partem Judiciorum."</note> Seventh: Elections. <note>original: "Septimo electiones." <term>Elections</term> is the branch of astrology used to determine the most auspicious moment to begin a specific activity, such as a war or a wedding.</note> Eighth: Revolutions. <note>original: "Octavo revolutiones." <term>Revolutions</term> (specifically solar revolutions) are charts cast for the exact moment the sun returns to its position at a person's birth, used to predict the events of the coming year.</note> Ninth: Nativities. <note>original: "Nono Nativitates." The study of individual birth charts.</note> Tenth: The revolutions of the times, or rains and showers. <note>original: "Decimo temporum revolutiones, seu Pluvias et Imbres." This refers to "natural" or meteorological astrology used to predict weather and seasonal changes.</note>

From this table of contents alone, one can see that we should expect anything but sound astronomical knowledge from Bonatti. In all appearances, the entire work is a collection of those astrological follies which the Arabs had already pushed to the extreme before him. Therefore, I do not see how Bandini, in his *Specimen of Florentine Literature* <note>Angelo Maria Bandini (1726–1803) was a famous Italian librarian and scholar.</note>, Volume 1, Preface page 30, and Mazzuchelli <note>Giammaria Mazzuchelli (1707–1765) was an Italian count and noted biographer of Italian writers.</note> following him, could credit Bonatti with the merit of being—alongside Paulus Geometra—the first to restore astronomy to its ancient splendor after the decline of Greek and Roman scholarship. They must have both understood "astrology" by that term.

Giovanni Pico della Mirandola judges him quite differently when he says in *Against Astrology*, Book 1: "I do not stoop to the more recent men, commoners and idiots, to whom as if to the rightful possessors almost the entire profession has devolved. Bonatti is of the primary authority among them; he is not only ignorant of philosophy, but furi—" <note>original Latin: "Ad juniores non descendo homines plebeos et idiotas ad quos quasi ad justos possessores tota fere profession devoluta est. Est Bonatus inter eos primae autoritatis; is non ignarus modo est Philosophiae, sed furi-" Pico della Mirandola was a brilliant Renaissance philosopher who wrote a famous 12-volume attack on astrology, viewing it as a superstition that undermined human free will.</note>

<header>### A Notorious Libertine.</header>

...[the soul] is left lacking the constraints of civil society. It is like a razor in the hand of a child. It hardly needs to be proven how much a disordered inclination toward the sensualities of the body is contrary to the principles, not only of true philosophy, but even of healthy, unlearned common sense. No type of folly brings punishment so immediately upon its heels as this one; and the loss of everything that human society holds dear—contempt, poverty, a sickly body, and only too often an early death—are in most cases the usual consequences of it.

Adrian Beverland was born in Middelburg, Zeeland, around 1652 or 1653; for since he was, according to de la Rue's assurance, about twenty-seven years old in 1680, he must have come into the world around this time. Nothing is known of his domestic circumstances; however, he must have come from a good family because, when he arrived in Oxford in 1672, he identified himself there as a Lord of Zeeland <note>original: "Dominum Zelandiae"</note>. Furthermore, in one of his letters, he calls Isaac Voss <note>A famous Dutch scholar and bibliophile who lived in England.</note>, his patron and protector, his maternal uncle <note>original: "Avunculum"</note>; therefore, his mother must have been the daughter of Gerard Johannes Vossius <note>One of the most famous scholars and humanists of the 17th century.</note>. He had a brother named Johann, to whom a letter from him still exists, though Johann’s profession is unknown; and in 1679, he had Bernhard de Gomme as a stepfather.

### 3. Hadrian Beverland,

From his youth, he displayed many talents, but he made the worst possible use of them. This was because he not only succumbed very early to the lowest debaucheries but also tuned his entire passion for ancient literature to this same frequency. He sought out only the most lascivious elements within it—and not merely seeking them out, but putting them into practice and imitating them. Ovid, Catullus, Petronius, and other writers of this sort were his favorites, and he committed the filthiest passages in their works to memory. He states himself in the dedication of his book *On the Law of Stoled Virginity* <note>original: "de stolatae virginitatis Jure." The title refers to the "stola," the traditional garment of a respectable Roman matron, making the title a provocative legal-erotic paradox.</note> that he had already compiled it in 1672, and thus in the twentieth year of his age. Presumably, the example of so many contemporary scholars at the Dutch universities, whose morals were not the purest, had a great influence on his development. Isaac Voss was no enemy of base pleasures, and Ulrich Huber <note>A highly influential Dutch jurist.</note>, a famous legal scholar at Franeker, even allowed the aforementioned shameful writing to be dedicated to him. He calls this Huber his teacher in the dedication dated July 18, 1679; therefore, it seems that he must have studied at Franeker, where Huber had been a professor since 1657.

His natural abilities must have developed very early; for when he stayed in Oxford in 1672—consequently in the twentieth year of his life—to make use of the library there, he had already written commentaries on Horace, Martial, Juvenal, and Petronius, which

# 3. Hadrian Beverland,

When he saw that his alleged reformation was not having as swift or as powerful an effect in Holland as he had perhaps hoped, he not only lost all inclination toward serious and respectable work, but he also completely returned to his former path. As early as 1698—according to the testimony of <term>Jacques Bernard</term> <note>Jacques Bernard (1658–1718) was a French theologian and journalist who took over the editorship of the *Nouvelles de la République des Lettres* from Pierre Bayle.</note> in the *News of the Republic of Letters* <note>original: "Nouvelles de la Rep. des Lettres," a major intellectual journal of the period.</note>, Oct. 1699, p. 468—he sent various manuscripts to Holland so that they might be printed there, including *Oxford Leisure* <note>original: "Otia Oxoniensia"</note>, *Notes on Martial* <note>original: "Notas in Martialem"</note>, *Notes on Juvenal* <note>original: "Juvenalem"</note>, etc., and *His English Journey* <note>original: "Iter suum Anglicum"</note>. However, Bernard was told that those to whom the manuscripts had been sent had burned them—a circumstance from which one can infer their scandalous content. 

From 1702 to 1709, he is found once again as the author of various libels <note>original: "Schmähschriften," which refers to defamatory or insulting pamphlets.</note>, which I shall list below. Since one of these was directed against three bishops who had spoken out against his lewd writings, it seems clear from this that he must have been circulating such material again. Because of this, he sank lower than ever in the estimation of all those who had previously supported him. As he now lost himself entirely among the ranks of the lowest libertines and dissolute characters, he was no longer thought of. ...ly wandered from one place to another, having lost his sanity, imagining that he was being pursued everywhere by two hundred people who had conspired to remove him from the world. It is suspected that he must have died in this state shortly after 1712, as nothing more was heard of him from that time onward. Such was the end of a man who, possessed of truly exceptional **genius**, could have become a worthy member of human society, had not the abuse of that talent led him to rebel against everything held sacred, to disregard all those restrictions on **sensuality** so necessary in civilized life, to disdain every serious and really useful application of his powers, and to seek the entire nourishment of his spirit in the dregs of the lowest debauchery. 

From his life and letters, one sees that he was nonetheless esteemed by many distinguished and learned men of his time, such as <term>Locke</term> <note>John Locke (1632–1704), the English philosopher known as the "Father of Liberalism."</note>, <term>Edward Brown</term> <note>Likely Edward Browne (1644–1708), a prominent English physician and traveler.</note>, <term>Pierre Bayle</term> <note>A French philosopher and pioneer of the Enlightenment (1647–1706).</note>, Friedrich Spanheim, Ulrich Huber, Jacob Gronovius, Nicolaas Heinsius, J. G. Graevius, and others, several of whom did not fail to provide him with sound advice and warnings. "I truly grieve," wrote <term>Graevius</term> <note>Johann Georg Graevius (1632–1703), a leading German classical scholar and critic.</note> among others to <term>Heinsius</term> <note>Nicolaas Heinsius the Elder (1620–1681), a famous Dutch scholar and poet.</note>, "for his lot, because he would not lend his ear to your and my wholesome warnings, and [his] talent..." <note>original Latin: "Doleo sane... vicem ejus, quod tuis meisque salutaribus monitis noluerit aures dare, et ingenium..."</note>

# 3. Hadrian Beverland,

1679, 157 pages in <term>octavo</term> <note>A standard book size in the 17th century, where a single sheet of paper was folded three times to create eight leaves (sixteen pages).</note>. This edition is expanded with a dedication to his stepfather Bernhard de Gomme and a letter to Jacob de Goyer, the latter of which is signed at Leiden on March 21, 1679. From this, it is evident that he arranged this edition while still in Leiden, and that it likely provided the occasion for the legal proceedings brought against him immediately afterward, because he had identified himself by name here. These are the only two editions of this writing that exist; for although August Beyer, in his *Critical Memoirs of Rare Books* <note>original Latin: "Memor. crit. libror. rar."</note> p. 225, cites two editions under the years 1670 and 1689, these are undoubtedly printing errors for 1678 and 1679. 

Meanwhile, Beyer had in his hands a copy from the former Bünau library—now the Electoral Library <note>Referring to the famous collection of Count Heinrich von Bünau, which later became part of the Saxon State Library in Dresden.</note>—which Beverland himself had intended for a third edition and had therefore provided with many handwritten additions. This edition was meant to bear the title: *Apples of Love, prepared by Hadrian Beverland, Licentiate of Laws. Third edition, more expanded and corrected than the previous ones. Ever Majestic* <note>original Latin: "Poma amoris per Hadr. Beverlandum, D V. Licent. adornata. Editio tertia prioribus auctior et emendatior. Semper Augustus."</note>. However, this version never appeared in print.

### 3. Hadrian Beverland,

1. *On the Brothels of the Ancients* <note>original Latin: "De prostibulis veterum." This was Beverland's most scandalous work, focusing on the history of ancient Roman sexuality and prostitution.</note>, for which he collected the most lewd engravings and other artworks at great expense, and from which Isaac Voss <note>Isaac Vossius (1618–1689), a renowned Dutch scholar and collector of ancient manuscripts who was a contemporary and associate of Beverland.</note>, as already mentioned, included some material in his *Catullus*. Various writers claim that when this work became known in Holland, the edition printed in Leiden was not permitted to be sold there, and so it was issued in London. However, although many copies bear "London" on the title page, there are indeed copies with the inscription: *Leiden, at Daniel van Gaesbeeck’s* <note>original Latin: "Lugd. Bat. ap. Dan. a Gaesbeck." "Lugdunum Batavorum" is the Latin name for the city of Leiden.</note>. See Hamberger’s *Reliable News* <note>original German: "Hambergers zuverl. Nachr." referring to Georg Christoph Hamberger’s *Zuverlässige Nachrichten von den vornehmsten Schriftstellern*.</note> Vol. 1, p. 474. It seems that this was Beverland’s favorite work; however, when he was forced by necessity to reconcile with his homeland, he—according to his own confession in his recantation—voluntarily sent his manuscript to Leiden to convince the University of the sincerity of his reformation. That it is still located there is clear from the *Catalogue of the University Library*, p. 333. Benthem <note>Heinrich Ludolf Benthem (1661–1723), a German theologian who documented the academic and social life of the Netherlands.</note> asserts that it was burned by one of his confidants during his arrest in Leiden; this may be the case, for it is certain that he was already working on it at that time, and it is at least not improbable that he took up this work again after his release.

For this reason, all true philosophers in all ages have honored the prevailing religion of their country, and not merely honored it, but often summoned the full strength of their philosophy to support and maintain it, whenever untimely impertinence <note>original: "unzeitiger Vorwitz," suggesting a meddling or intrusive curiosity that oversteps its bounds.</note> sought to undermine it under the pretext of **Enlightenment**. It is well known how much effort Leibniz made to adapt some of its doctrines to **Reason**.

Johann Christian Edelmann was of this sort. He was born on the 9th—or according to others, the 11th—of July, 1698, at Weissenfels, where his father Gottlob, who originated from Mark-Lissa in Upper Lusatia, was tutor to the court pages and a chamber musician to the Duke, later receiving the title of Secretary and dying at Eisenach. He was the eldest of his father's three sons; of the others, one had dedicated himself to the law, while the other was a painter and resided in Gotha around 1732. His father also had two brothers, one of whom, Gottfried, was a preacher at Lauban, while the other, Christian, was a chamber administrator at Weissenfels. In his youth, our subject <note>The author uses "our subject" or "ours" (der unsrige) to refer to Edelmann, the focus of the biography.</note> enjoyed a good education, attending schools in Lauban, Altenburg, and Weissenfels, and in 1720 he went to Jena, where he dedicated himself to theology. Since his talents were only of a very ordinary kind, and his diligence extended no further than what his future destination as a preacher seemed to require, the knowledge he harvested there was in no way distinguished. Nevertheless, in 1724 he defended his thesis twice under Master Adolph Janzen *on the Passover of Christ* <note>original Latin: "de paschate Christi," a standard theological topic concerning the historical and ritual aspects of the biblical Passover.</note>. At the same time, his entire negotiation with the Herrnhuters <note>Members of the Moravian Church.</note> fell through, and although the causes are not precisely known, it seems that with his vehement and stubborn character, he was not flexible enough for the Count, while the latter was not compliant enough to grant the advances of money requested by the former.

Around 1741, he wrote as a farewell the **Prepared Blows for the Fool’s Back**, in which he exposed the weaknesses of this sect with his characteristic insolence.

Edelmann, who had by now wandered through several desolate places, now drew ever closer to <term>Naturalism: A philosophical system that excludes supernatural explanations, viewing the world through the lens of natural laws and reason.</term>, as in that very same year he published not only his **Moses with Uncovered Face**, but also his **Christ and Belial**. In the first work, he seeks primarily to make the inspiration of the Holy Scriptures appear ridiculous; in the second, however, he seeks to ridicule the <term>Satisfaction of Christ: The theological doctrine that Christ’s suffering and death satisfied divine justice for human sin.</term>. I say "to make ridiculous," for neither work can claim the name of a serious disputation, neither in regard to the arguments used nor in their tone—the latter being, as in all of Edelmann’s writings, extremely uncouth and offensive.

He had, by all appearances, composed these writings while still in Berleburg; however, his stay here had now come to an end. Count Casimir died on June 5, 1741, and since his son and successor, Count Ludwig Ferdinand, held different views regarding unrestricted tolerance...

In 1742, or perhaps as early as 1741, he published his *Divinity of Reason*, which he intended to take the place of the rejected Bible. However, in doing so, he fell into an opposite kind of <note>The German term "Schwärmerey" refers to excessive, often fanatical religious enthusiasm or "fanaticism," a common 18th-century criticism for those seen as too radical.</note> religious fervor: he portrayed Reason as a part and an outpouring of the divine essence, not essentially different from God Himself. Consequently, he interpreted everything said in the Gospel of John regarding the <term>Logos: <note>original: "λογος"</note> The Greek word for "Word" or "Reason," traditionally used in theology to describe the divine nature of Christ.</term> or "Word" as referring to human Reason. Based on this line of thought, he also abstained from eating meat for a time, because in his opinion, the souls of animals must also be outpourings of the divinity.

Edelmann moved from Hachenburg to Neuwied, where the authorities were willing to protect him but did not want to grant him unrestricted tolerance; he was therefore ordered to set down his confession of faith in writing. He presented part of it on July 23, 1745, to the local <term>consistory: A governing body of the church responsible for maintaining doctrine and discipline.</term>, and on September 1st to the Count himself. At the same time, he promised neither to share the document with anyone in writing nor to further spread his teachings. Presumably, he kept neither of these promises, for shortly thereafter, in 1746, his confession of faith was published in Frankfurt along with a refutation. Since his base insults had turned everyone against him who still honored morality and social propriety, he had only himself to blame for the fact that, for a considerable time, he could no longer find a permanent residence. Instead, he had to stay here and there, secretly and anonymously, among his few friends and followers. ### a well-known scoffer of religion.

hann Christian Edelmann, both full of the most uncivilized insults, not only against the Provost but against the whole Christian and especially the Lutheran church. Through this, he drew the attention of the authorities in these regions, who had his confession of faith confiscated in Hamburg. Meanwhile, the Imperial Prosecutor <term>Reichs-Fiscal; the chief legal official responsible for protecting the interests of the Holy Roman Empire</term> had also begun to take action against him. He realized that he needed a more powerful sanctuary and believed he would find it in Berlin; he traveled there in 1747 and immediately began to spread his opinions and teachings wherever he could. Since he had taken up residence in the parish of Provost Süssmilch <note>Johann Peter Süssmilch (1707–1767), a prominent German clergyman and a pioneer of demography, famous for his work on "The Divine Order."</note>, the latter felt obligated to warn his congregation against this man. This was a thunderbolt for him, though one he had certainly prepared for himself through his own indiscretions. He lived in these circumstances until February 15, 1767, when he died at the age of 69.

### 5. Nicolaus Barnaud or Bernaud, a Gold-maker *)

The love of gold very early on led mankind into the folly of attempting to imitate this highly esteemed metal through art <term>Ars; here referring to the "art" of alchemy</term>, and thereby increasing its quantity. Viewed theoretically, it does not seem to be so utterly impossible to dissolve natural bodies into their primary constituents, to examine them, and then to imitate nature’s own process to produce bodies that are at least similar to hers. In this way, art has succeeded in imitating some types of gemstones quite skillfully; although there remains a very great difference between the imitation of these stones and the production of artificial metals that are completely identical to natural ones.

Should this imitation ever be possible regarding metals, one would have to begin with the lighter and more imperfect metals—for example, iron—stealing nature’s own methods from it and progressing imperceptibly to the more perfect metals. However, human greed believes it cannot afford to take so many steps; it ventures directly toward the most perfect thing the inanimate world of matter has to offer, and without [understanding] its nature and

### 5. Nicolas Barnaud,

In order to know its delicate web <note>The "web" refers to the intricate workings of nature mentioned on the previous page</note>, humanity makes a thousand attempts to defy nature and to develop her secrets even against her will. Worse still, this folly commonly turns into such an addiction that it rarely ends in anything but the total ruin of the one whom it has infected; and when such a person finally sees himself deceived, he seeks to deceive others as well, shrouding himself in mysterious language because he knows this is the surest bait for the simple-minded and the ignorant. It is true that there are examples of seemingly successful experiments which carry much appearance of truth; yet even the most remarkable among them are not free from the suspicion of a played-out fraud, which in many other cases is undeniable.

One of these deceptive teachers of the so-called Great Work <term>Great Work; original: *großen Werkes*, also known as the *Magnum Opus*, the alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone to transmute base metals into gold</term>, who deceived countless gullible fools at least in his own fatherland, is Nicolas Barnaud. He is a writer whose life circumstances are very little known, appearing around the beginning of the previous century <note>the early 1600s</note>. One finds him named sometimes Barnaud, sometimes Bernaud, which has led many otherwise very precise writers to mistake him for two different people. Hendreich, in his *Pandects* <note>original: *pandectis*; referring to Christoph Hendreich’s *Pandectae Brandenburgicae*, a massive 17th-century bibliographic encyclopedia</note>, even transforms him into three distinct persons, whom he calls Barnaudus, Bernaudus, and Bernardus. Many claim him to be a citizen of Geneva because he lived there for several years; however, since he himself in his own writings—

->a gold-maker.<-

Since some call him a "Delphinate from Crest Arnaudi" <note>original: *Delphinatem a Crista Arnaudi*; a Latinized reference to his birthplace in the Dauphiné region</note>, it is undeniable that he was a native of Crest, a small town in the Dauphiné, where he must have been born around 1535. He was actually a physician; however, since most of his writings concern alchemy, he does not seem to have advanced very far in the former art <note>meaning the art of medicine</note>. According to his own assertions, he was in Spain around 1559, though it remains unknown for what occasion or purpose. He identified with the Reformed religion <note>Protestantism</note>, and therefore, following the infamous St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre, he published his *Wake-Up Call* <note>original: *Reveil-Matin*; a political pamphlet titled *Le Réveille-matin des Français*</note> in Geneva in 1574, in which he told the King and Queen the bitterest truths. For this reason, Lasin—the stepbrother or brother-in-law of Beauvais-le-Nocle—who encountered him in the street in Basel the following year, felt compelled to avenge the honor of his court by slapping Barnaud’s face.

Yet Barnaud was not discouraged from publishing satires on the French constitution of that time, provided that the writings subsequently attributed to him are indeed his own. He was later accused not only of Arianism <term>Arianism; a theological doctrine maintaining that Jesus Christ was distinct from and subordinate to God the Father, considered a major heresy by both the Catholic and Reformed churches</term>, but was also suspected of being the author of the notorious book *The Three Impostors* <note>original: *de tribus Impostoribus*; a legendary and highly controversial book that allegedly claimed Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad were all deceivers</note>. The latter accusation is absurd, because this book—if it indeed exists at all—is much older than Barnaud. Furthermore, the entire claim stems from a passage in a rare book,

He resided in Geneva between 1575 and 1599, but moved to Leiden in the latter year, and in 1601 to Gouda, where he presumably died. This is everything known about him, and his name would likely have been forgotten by posterity—neither remembered as a physician nor as a friend of Socinus—had he not kept his memory alive among the lovers of the **Great Art** <term>Great Art; a traditional name for Alchemy, specifically the pursuit of the Philosopher's Stone</term> through various alchemical writings, which he seems to have written especially in the final years of his life. ### 6. Joseph Francis Borro,

born in Milan on May 4th, 1625, had as his father **Branda Borro**, a famous physician <note>original: *Arzt*</note> of his time *), who [wrote] some Latin

Another short report is attached to Borro's *Key to the Cabinet* <note>original Italian: *Chiave del Gavinetto*</note>, Cologne (Geneva), 1681, 12mo. From these sources I have compiled this current biography; I shall cite in the following sections, in their proper places, some other writings which mention him in passing or provide only individual circumstances of his life. Almost all writers outside of Italy call him Borri; Corte, Mazzuchelli, and others, on the other hand, call him Borro. Since he called himself **Burrhus** in Latin, the latter form is the correct one. Had he been named Borri in his mother tongue, he would have had to call himself *de Burrhis* in Latin. Some of the writers cited above list his birth in 1627; however, since the most reliable sources attribute to him an age of 70 years, and 1695 is beyond dispute as the year of his death, he must have been born in 1625.</margin>

### 6. Giuseppe Francesco Borri <note>original: "Joseph Franc. Borro"</note>

to deal with the animals according to the degree of their wickedness; the souls of these wild animals were also taken from evil spirits, and so forth. One can easily imagine that he did not allow for any lack of revelations <note>claims of divine or supernatural communication</note> in this matter either. # a Gold-maker and Charlatan.

continuation of the trial. Borri was summoned on March 20, 1659, under penalty of the greater excommunication <note>original: *grossern Bannes*; a severe form of exclusion from the Catholic Church</note> to appear within 90 days and give an account of himself, while at the same time a safe conduct was promised to him. Since he did not appear, he was publicly declared under the greater excommunication after the 90 days had passed. As even this would not move him to return, he was summoned for the last time on October 20, 1660, to appear within 90 days and hear the final judgment pronounced over him. This judgment stated that, as a heretic, he was guilty of all the ecclesiastical and secular penalties established for such crimes; therefore, he was declared to have forfeited all honors and privileges and was excluded from the community of the Church. All of his assets were to fall to the Treasury <note>original: *Fisco*</note>, and his image, along with his godless writings, were to be publicly burned. This sentence was publicly executed on January 2, 1661, on the Campo de' Fiori <note>a famous square in Rome used for public executions</note> \*) and was repeated soon after on March 17/27 in Milan, during which the Pope promised fifteen years of indulgence <note>the remission of temporal punishment for sin</note> to all those who would attend as spectators. The writings burned with his image were merely written essays, which

### a Goldmaker and Charlatan.

Borri had saved himself from Milan by flight; however, the first location to which he turned is not recorded. In the sentence of the Inquisition, it is merely stated that he had traveled to a certain city named in the records \*) and did not hesitate to spread some of the aforementioned religious delusions <note>German: *Schwärmereyen*; a term often used in this period to describe radical or "enthusiastic" religious deviancy</note> anew. He reportedly taught there, among other things, that one was not obligated to reveal secret sins during confession. Most of his biographers are content to say generally that after his flight, he traveled through Austria (others substitute Switzerland for this) to Strasbourg. However, it is certain that Innsbruck was at least the first German town where he stayed after his flight from Italy—at least as long as his misfortunes were not yet known there. Yet, he presumably soon realized here as well that he would not make his fortune with a new religion; therefore, he now took recourse to his two remaining expedients: quackery...

---

\*) Perhaps it was Padua; for the fact that he was once there as well is evident from a letter by an anonymous correspondent to Doctor <term>Sebiz</term> <note>Melchior Sebiz (1584–1674) was a celebrated physician and professor in Strasbourg.</note>, in which the writer assures him that <term>Borri</term> had sufficiently demonstrated his incompetence in chemical experiments in Padua by breaking many distillation vessels. <note>original Latin: *Patavii Dominus CAROLUS OFFREDI certiorem me fecit, BURRUM Patavii multa rumpendo et frangendo vasa destillatoria satis declarasse, quantum noverit ignis regere gradus, et quantum excellat in Alchymia.*</note> "In Padua, Lord <term>CARLO OFFREDI</term> informed me that <term>BORRI</term>, by breaking and shattering many distillation vessels in Padua, has sufficiently declared how well he knows how to control the degrees of fire, and how much he 'excels' in alchemy." <term>Schelhorn’s</term> *Literary Delights*, Vol. 5, p. 144.

### 6. Joseph Franc. Borro,

...was assembled. Borro was led onto the scaffold with his hands bound, between which he held a burning wax candle. There, kneeling, he had to repeat the abjuration <note>A formal public renunciation of his alleged "heretical" beliefs and magical practices.</note> that was read to him. After its conclusion, he was required to thank the Inquisition for the lenient punishment. The mournful pageantry surrounding him caused him to faint twice during the ceremony. After it had concluded, he was led back to his prison. A few days later, under similar ceremonies, the second part of his sentence was made known to him. This part condemned him to perpetual imprisonment <note>original: "ewige Gefängniß," literally eternal prison; in practice, a life sentence.</note>, during which he was to pray the Christian Creed <note>The Apostles' Creed or Nicene Creed, used here as a corrective penance.</note> once every day and the seven Penitential Psalms <note>A traditional set of seven psalms (6, 32, 38, 51, 102, 130, and 143) used in the Catholic Church to express sorrow for sins.</note> once every week. Furthermore, he was to wear the garment of the Inquisition <note>The *sanbenito*, a yellow tunic worn by those convicted by the Inquisition as a sign of public shame.</note> for the rest of his life, marked with a red cross on the chest and the back *).

Borro’s imprisonment in Rome caused a great sensation everywhere. Since there were still enough gullible people, even among the nobility, who credited him with superior knowledge, there was no shortage of people who visited him in his confinement. However, the permission of a Cardinal was always necessary for such a visit. Among these visitors was the Duke d'Estrées <note>César d'Estrées (1628–1714), a French diplomat and Cardinal who was often involved in the high-stakes politics of the Roman court.</note>, who lay ill with a dangerous sickness—

# a Goldmaker and Charlatan.

...lay ill, and had already been given up by the doctors. This man finally placed his trust in Borri and obtained permission for him to visit; he was successfully restored to health by him, whereupon it was jokingly said that an arch-heretic had performed a great miracle in Rome. However, how often have mere empirics <term>Empirics: from the Latin "empyrici," these were medical practitioners who relied on practical experience and trial-and-error rather than formal university education; they were often dismissed as "quacks" by licensed physicians.</term>, with the audacity typical of such people, performed similar miracles by attempting cures at random? When ten such cures fail in this manner, one is ashamed to have employed them, and covers their incompetence, one's own shame, and the deceased with earth; but if by chance one succeeds, it is exalted as a miracle.

Be that as it may, this fortunate cure made his fortune, as far as a prisoner of the Inquisition can be fortunate. The Duke d’Estrées <note>César d'Estrées (1628–1714), a powerful French Cardinal and diplomat who likely valued Borri’s alchemical and medical skills.</note> secured for him a more tolerable imprisonment in the Castel Sant’Angelo <note>original: "Engelsburg," the fortress in Rome used as a refuge and prison for the Papacy.</note>, where three rooms were assigned to him, and he was also permitted to perform laboratory work <note>original: "Laboriren," referring to alchemical or chemical experiments.</note>. At the same time, he had permission to go as far as a certain door in the middle of the stairs of the tower in the Castel Sant’Angelo, where strangers could speak with him. Queen Christina <note>Christina of Sweden (1626–1689), the former queen who moved to Rome and was a famous patron of science and alchemy.</note>, who remembered her former acquaintance with him, had him brought to her several times as long as she lived and conversed with him. ### 7. Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli <note>original: "Joh. Aurelius Augurelli."</note>

...deceived no one but himself. He was at the same time a Latin poet—two qualities that are very easily combined, because the inclination toward alchemy <note>original: "Goldmacherey," literally "gold-making."</note> only too often has its foundation in an overactive imagination.

He was a native of Rimini; therefore, according to the custom of his time, he is called by many simply Giovanni Aurelio of Rimini. Since shortly after his time there was a noble family of this name in that place—from which Lodovico <note>original: "Ludwig."</note>, a son of Antonio <note>original: "Anton."</note> Augurelli, was a councilor to Sigismondo Malatesta <note>The Malatesta family were the sovereign rulers of Rimini.</note> and was admitted among the city’s hundred nobles in 1509—it seems that he was of noble birth. However, the fact that our subject had a brother named Girolamo <note>original: "Hieronymus."</note> seems to weigh against this connection. Girolamo must have been a mere craftsman, because his son Pietro Paolo <note>original: "Petrus Paulus."</note>, a goldsmith, was admitted to the council of Rimini in 1509. Mazzuchelli <note>Giammaria Mazzuchelli (1707–1765) was a famous Italian count and biographer known for his massive work on Italian writers.</note> suspects, however, that one branch of this family (from which the aforementioned Lodovico came) had elevated itself to the nobility in one way or another, while the others—including our subject—remained in the middle class <note>original: "bürgerlichen."</note>. The noble branch of Lodovico died out shortly thereafter, but descendants of Girolamo were still present in 1616.

The date of his birth is not precisely specified; however, from a passage in his poems

# a Gold-Maker.

...it can be conjectured that he must have been born around 1454. His poems were published by, among others, Aldus in Venice in 1505. The 25th poem of the first book of *Iambics* <note>original: "Iambic." referring to Augurelli's *Iambici Libri*.</note> in this edition is addressed to Aldus, and in it he asks him to oversee, correct, and ensure his poems are printed accurately. It begins as follows:

> Aldus, the things our little book contains were begun when six lustra <note>A *lustrum* is a Roman unit of time lasting five years; thus, six lustra signifies he was thirty years old. Original: "Vitae peractis, Alde, sex lustris mihi / Sunt coepta, noster quae libellus continet."</note> of my life had passed; they were finished, however, shortly after ten lustra <note>Ten lustra signifies fifty years of age. Original: "Perfecta vero lustra post paulo decem, etc."</note>, etc.

If one assumes that Aldus printed his poems in the very same year they were sent to him, Augurelli was nearly 50 years old in 1505; consequently, 1454 would be his birth year. To be sure, there is an even earlier edition of his poems from 1491; however, as Mazzuchelli assures us, the aforementioned poem is not found in that one, meaning he must have composed it only for the second edition.

Some circumstances of his life can be gleaned from his poems. It is clear from them that he studied in Padua in his youth, stayed there for a long time, and also received citizenship there. \*) From there he went to Treviso <note>original: "Trevigio."</note>, where he likewise received citizenship and at the same time a canonry <note>A canonry is a beneficial position within a cathedral or collegiate church.</note>, which—

### a gold-maker.

Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552) was an Italian physician and historian known for his biographical sketches of famous men.</note> assures us that he was considered the most learned and sincere among all those who gave instruction in Venice at that time. Bembo, Navagero <note>Andrea Navagero (1483–1529), a Venetian poet, orator, and diplomat.</note>, and Lippomani <note>Girolamo Lippomano, a member of a prominent Venetian family and a student of the humanities.</note> were his pupils here. However, Augurelli earned merit not only in ancient literature but also in his mother tongue <note>The Italian vernacular.</note>, being one of the first to teach how to write it correctly and purely; for this reason, Bembo <note>Pietro Bembo (1470–1547) was a central figure in the development of the Italian language.</note> called him his "father" and submitted the first two books of his work on the Italian language <note>Likely referring to the *Prose della volgar lingua*, a foundational text for Italian grammar and style.</note> to his review. Hieronymus Avanzi <note>Girolamo Avanzi, a scholar from Verona known for editing Latin classics.</note> did the same regarding his emendations of Catullus (Venice, 1500 and 1520, Folio), which is preceded by Avanzi’s letter to Augurelli.

From all this, it is clear that Augurelli was a learned and, in his time, a quite renowned man; however, he greatly obscured his merit through a prevailing inclination toward alchemy, which went so far with him that he incessantly distilled and boiled, seeking to transform mercury into silver and silver into gold \*). However, he achieved nothing more by this than making himself poor and destitute <meta>catchword: read</meta>

---

\*) "Lastly, that ridiculous disease—the companion of certain poverty and fruitless labor, familiar to curious minds—occupied the poor little man entirely, as he re-boiled metals and juices in hidden furnaces, so that he might produce solid and ductile silver from mercury for the minting of coins, and by smelting a wondrous mass of nature's hidden things, create pure gold therefrom." <note>original Latin: "Novissime ridendus ille morbus certae egestatis, et cassi laboris comes, curiosis ingeniis familiaris, totum homunculum occupavit, metalla et succos in abditis fornacibus recoquentem, ut ex argento vivum concretum et ductile argentum, ad cudendam monetam efficeret, et admirabilem abditarum naturae rerum massam conflando, purum inde aurum crearetur."</note> Jovius in *Eulogies of Learned Men*, p. 159, Antwerp edition, 1557, octavo.

### 6. Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli,

...labored, without being cured of his affliction <note>The author refers to Augurelli's obsession with alchemy as a "sickness" or "affliction."</note> by the losses he sustained. For after he could no longer continue his labors due to a lack of wealth, he composed the Latin poem *Chrysopoeia* <note>Original: *Chrysopoeia*, from the Greek words for "gold" and "making."</note>, so famous among the adepts <term>Adept: In the context of alchemy, an individual who has attained the secret of transmuting base metals into gold.</term>, in which he not only asserted in all seriousness the possibility of the transmutation of metals, but also described at length the entire process of preparing the Philosopher's Stone.

To present alchemy poetically might seem strange to some; fundamentally, however, it is not, as the usual language of the gold-makers is already half-poetry anyway, being a mixture of incomprehensible tropes and allegories. Another, though later, gold-boiler <note>A "gold-boiler" or *Goldkocher* was a common derisive term for an alchemist who spent their time over a furnace.</note>, Johann Nicolaus Furich, likewise presented this "great art" in his *Chryseidos* <note>Original: *Chryseidos libr. IV*, Strasbourg, 1631, quarto.</note> in the form of a Latin poem, and such rhymed alchemical processes are not lacking in other languages either.

To compensate at least somewhat for the losses suffered through this art, Augurelli dedicated his poem to Pope Leo X, who reigned from 1513 to 1521 and was known for his luxury and extravagance. He hoped to receive a rich reward from the Pope for the discovery of the Philosopher's Stone, but he was greatly deceived—either because the Pope saw through the folly of the entire art, or because he had more convenient and reliable means of making gold <note>This likely alludes to the Pope's collection of church tithes and the controversial sale of indulgences.</note>, and therefore the artist...

# a Gold-Maker.

### 7. Giovanni Aurelio Augurelli

...the mass gradually dissolves, and its vapors rise into the glass flask—initially white, but afterwards sky-blue or violet. From this you can prepare two kinds of tinctures: one for the dissolution of gold, and the other for the refinement of oriental pearls. If you wish to augment this tincture even further, so that it transforms base metals into the purest gold, then put it into a small glass vessel, seal it, and place it over an unquenchable lamp <note>An "unquenchable lamp" refers to a constant heat source maintained for long durations, essential for the slow "cooking" of the alchemical substance during the "Great Work."</note>; thus many colors will appear at the outer edge of the glass. Initially the mass appears black, then brown, then dark red, and so on. After 44 days and nights, the white color appears, and then one is near the goal of one’s desires. Then take a pound of mercury, bring it into the fire, and as soon as it begins to smoke, add your white mass to it; the mercury will transform into a fixed silver <term>Fixed silver: In alchemical theory, "fixed" refers to a substance that has become stable and can withstand heat without vaporizing, unlike raw mercury.</term>. Place this over the aforementioned lamp, and the white color will turn into a bright yellow saffron color, and after the course of a year, into a deep red purple color—and now one has the blessed powder, with which one can not only transform all metals into gold, but also heal all diseases."

Let one judge for oneself whether such a process is still worth even a silk purse <note>A callback to the previous page's anecdote where Pope Leo X gave Augurelli an empty silk purse as a "reward" for his poem.</note>. Even considered as poetry, it is hardly worth it, as it is extremely cold, sluggish, and prosaic.

# a Goldmaker.

...even though the subject matter allows for a high degree of liveliness.

The exact time of his death is not known with certainty. Jovius <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian physician, historian, and biographer known for his works on famous men.</note> says merely that he died in the 83rd year of his age. If 1454 was the year of his birth, then according to this statement, 1537 must have been the year of his death. He died suddenly in Treviso <note>original: "Trevigio"</note> in a bookstore and was buried in the cathedral there, specifically with the following epitaph composed by himself, which, however, no longer exists:

> This is the image of AURELIUS AUGURELLUS which you see,
> A man devoted to serious literary study
> And to playful jests, though with unequal care:
> The former so that he might become more vigorous for serious tasks,
> The latter so that he might be more steady when engaging in play.

### 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

[...his] own wife [told] the subsequent Saxe-Gotha Chief Mining Inspector <term>Ober-Berg-Inspector: a high-ranking official overseeing mining operations, a vital industry in the 17th-century German states</term> Friedrich Heyn, who accompanied Becher on his travels in England and also attended his funeral in 1682, that despite her husband's pretenses, she knew well that he could not be far from 60 years of age. It is therefore more than probable that Becher, out of vanity, represented himself as younger than he truly was, and that he must have been born at least between 1622 and 1625. The following history will confirm this even further. Also, his portrait painted in Vienna in 1675, which has been engraved several times, looks more like a man in his fifties than one in his forties.

Becher's father was, according to the son's claim, a great polymath <note>original: "Gedächtnißgelehrter," literally a 'memory scholar,' referring to someone with an encyclopedic command of information</note>, who by the 28th year of his age understood ten languages—namely Hebrew, Chaldean, Samaritan, Syriac, Arabic, Greek, Latin, German, Dutch, and Italian—and had written many hundreds of sheets <term>Bogen: standard printer's sheets used to measure the length of a manuscript</term> concerning them. The son wished to yield nothing to him in this regard, and this might have been one of the reasons why he later made himself ten years younger in his *Method of Teaching* <note>original: "Methodo didactica"</note>, in which he boasts of this about his father.

Of his youth we know nothing except what he himself mentions in his writings, and especially in the aforementioned *Method of Teaching* and *Psychosophy* <note>original: "Psychosophie"</note>, which, however, is very un— <note>The text breaks off mid-word; likely "unzuverlässig" (unreliable) or "unvollständig" (incomplete)</note>

# 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

[As soon as] he was finished with this <note>referring to his study of theology mentioned on the previous page</note>, he supposedly learned mathematics, after that medicine, and finally chemistry. Through his interest in mathematics, he became acquainted with several crafts, and the practices of these crafts led him into law and politics; thus, in a few years, he had taught himself nearly all the sciences.

If one discounts the characteristic tendency toward self-praise which Becher used to exaggerate, magnify, or perhaps even invent in the history of his studies and his youth, it is clear that he received a poor education and, despite his great talents, studied in a very disorganized manner. It is in these two circumstances that the foundation of all his subsequent fates is to be found. At which university he actually studied—or rather, where he resided, since by his own account he learned everything from himself and very little from others—is just as unknown as all other circumstances regarding the time and place of his early life. That he was finally in Mainz and became a Doctor <note>likely a Doctor of Medicine, though Becher's qualifications were often questioned by his rivals</note> there is quite certain; however, before we can accompany him there, we must first see him wander through a large part of Germany and even Europe.

the words included therein followed in alphabetical order; in the following columns followed the equivalent words of other languages, as many as one desired. The words in the Latin column were marked with numbers. If one wished, for example, to correspond with a Russian whose language one did not understand, and who also did not understand the writer's language, one only had to look up the words in the Latin column and write down the number found with each one in sequence. The receiver looked up the number in his dictionary <note>original: *Lexico*</note> and the corresponding word in the Russian column, and thus he understood the sender. This was nothing less than a universal language—not even a universal script—but only a kind of steganography <term>Steganography: the practice of hiding a secret message within a non-secret one; here, using numbers as a code</term>, which could also remain so no longer than the aforementioned dictionary was not in many hands. ### 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

...seen as nothing less than depriving all merchants and manufacturers of their livelihood in order to enrich the court and its flatterers. ### 8. Johann Joachim Becher.

Greed led him in 1672 to lead the Counts of Pöttingen to believe that he possessed the secret of extracting one gold <term>Ducat: A gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe, known for its high purity</term> weekly from one <term>Mark: A traditional unit of weight for precious metals, roughly equivalent to 234 grams</term> of fine silver, such that the silver would lose nothing of its quality or weight. He offered to reveal the secret to them if they would guarantee him 120 ducats weekly from the gold obtained. Although the Counts accepted this condition and a formal contract was drawn up—which Becher himself had printed \*)—it does not appear that the matter ever came to fruition; undoubtedly because Becher, as was his custom, had boasted of more scientific knowledge than he actually possessed.

Of a similar nature was the plan which he presented to the Hanau court a few years earlier, namely in 1669, by reviving the project for a West Indian colony which he had already set in motion in Munich. He had presumably become acquainted with the extravagant Count Friedrich Casimir of Hanau during one of the journeys he was obliged to take to Holland on behalf of the Viennese court. # 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

undertook the establishment of this institution <note>The "workhouse and manufactory" mentioned on the previous page, designed as a state-sponsored industrial hub</note> at his own expense, and the management was entrusted to Becher. For a time, perhaps at Becher’s instigation, there was indecision as to whether Count von Sinzendorf, the President of the Chamber <term>President of the Chamber: (German: "Kammer-Präsident") The head of the Hofkammer, the central financial and administrative body of the Habsburg Monarchy</term>, whose department actually oversaw manufacturing and trade matters, should be involved or not. Meanwhile, he surreptitiously sabotaged the institution whenever he could. Through his pride and impetuous nature, Becher simultaneously made enemies of the Chamber commissioners overseen by the institution—Salo and Cascher—and nearly all the subordinate officials. Furthermore, because he provided ample opportunity for criticism through his disorderly lifestyle—being accused of gambling, drinking, and other excesses—the directorship was eventually stripped from him.

### 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

The merits attributed to him regarding the manufacturing and financial systems seem to have the greatest appearance of validity; yet, when one duly considers everything, one must significantly lower the tone here as well. Immediately following the Thirty Years’ War <note>The Thirty Years' War (1618–1648) left the German states economically devastated and depopulated, prompting rulers to seek new ways to generate wealth.</note>, almost all German courts turned their attention toward manufacturing and commerce in order to fill the gaps that the long, ruinous war had created in the prosperity of the lands. 

This prevailing sentiment was exploited, as always, by "project makers" <term>Projectmacher</term> <note>A term often used disparagingly in the 17th and 18th centuries for speculators or "idea men" who proposed ambitious but often impractical schemes for economic improvement.</note> of all kinds, and Becher was one of them. In this, he was not even one of the first, for all the Upper German <note>Referring to the southern regions of Germany, such as Bavaria and Austria.</note> courts had already been occupied with the matter before him; he did nothing more than join in the chorus, and since he had seen and experienced much in foreign countries, many good designs were bound to be among the many immature ones. 

One must therefore be very inexperienced in German history if one wishes to continue asserting—along with almost all Cameralist <term>Cameralistische</term> <note>Cameralism was the German science of administration and economic policy, focusing on increasing the state's wealth and power through taxation and trade regulation.</note> writers—that Becher was the first to open the eyes of the Germans regarding the manufacturing and commercial systems. The eyes of the Germans had been opened long before Becher; the Thirty Years’ War had opened them, and all that was lacking was a man to direct them toward the right point; but Becher was not even that man, because he, like so many other Cameralists of this period, [treated] the factories and trade

# 8. Johann Joachim Becher,

**47.** During his stay in Vienna, Becher had drafted a manuscript regarding the interests of the imperial hereditary lands <note>the ancestral territories of the House of Habsburg, primarily in modern-day Austria, Slovenia, and parts of the Czech Republic</note> and intended to have it printed, but he could not obtain permission from the imperial court to do so. Long afterward, the well-known work appeared: ***Austria Over All, If She Only Wills It*** <note>original: *Oesterreich über alles, wenn es nur will*</note>, which was reprinted in 1750 and is attributed to Becher’s brother-in-law, Paul Wilhelm von Hörnigk. This same Hörnigk also published the ***Historical Report on the Privileges of the Most Noble Archducal House of Austria*** <note>original: *historische Anzeige von denen Privilegiis des hochlöbl. Erzhauses Oesterreich*</note>, Regensburg, 1708, octavo, though he identified himself there only with the initials P. W. v. H. It is possible, and even probable, that Becher’s aforementioned manuscript forms the basis of this work, if it is not the very same text—at least according to the first edition, for it was expanded in the second.

### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

...finished his studies and returned again to Moravia. It does not appear, therefore, that he enjoyed a proper academic education, and this deficiency explains his later eccentric whims <note>German: *Grillen*; refers to idiosyncratic or fanciful ideas</note> to reform all sciences and branches of knowledge and to restrict them to his own small store of the same. Shortly after his return—and, it seems, as early as 1614—he became Rector <note>A headmaster or high-ranking educational official</note> at Prerau <note>Modern Přerov, Czech Republic</note>, the capital of the district named after it in Moravia. In 1616, he became a preacher there, but in 1618 he became a preacher and Rector at Fulnek, another small town in that same district. It was here very early on that he began to concern himself with the improvement of school instruction, particularly in making the learning of languages easier for the youth and in combining the knowledge of things <note>The pedagogical concept of "Realien"—learning about the physical world and practical objects alongside vocabulary</note> with the study of words. However, he also expressed many strange opinions very early on, especially regarding physics; for his *Divine Theater* <note>original German: *göttlicher Schauplatz*</note>, which he published as early as 1616, already contained the material for his *Mosaic Physics* <note>A system of natural philosophy based on the biblical account of creation in the books of Moses</note>, which he set forth more elaborately several years later. During this time—that is, from 1614 to 1621—he must also have completed the map of Moravia, which I shall mention among his writings in what follows.

Comenius's efforts toward the improvement of school instruction were certainly praiseworthy and beneficial, and they reveal a mind that, at least in one respect, saw and thought clearly.

The city of **Fulnek** was plundered and burned to the ground in 1621, on which occasion Comenius lost not only his possessions but also all his books and writings. The Protestant clergy were driven out everywhere and banished from the entire land by a formal edict in August 1624. ### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

taught. He himself lacked the necessary philosophical concepts, and since the <term>peripatetic philosophy</term> <note>The traditional philosophy based on Aristotle that dominated universities at the time.</note> common at that time was too difficult for him, he sought a lighter and more convenient source of knowledge, which he found in the Mosaic account of creation <note>The biblical story of the beginning of the world in Genesis.</note>. According to this, he assumed three principles <note>original: *Principia*</note> or fundamental essences of all things: matter, spirit, and light. To him, matter is a lifeless physical entity into which the Spirit of God breathed the first world-spirit <note>original: *Weltgeist*</note> to enliven and move it. Man consists of three parts: the body, which is mortal; the spirit, which as a part of the world-spirit dissipates at death; and the soul, which is from God and lives eternally, and so forth. *). Comenius was certainly not the inventor of this Mosaic philosophy, but he was one of the first to give it prestige—a prestige caused not so much by his own erudition as by the applause his *Janua* <note>Referring to his famous language textbook *Janua linguarum reserata* (The Door of Tongues Unlocked).</note> received everywhere. Moreover, it was convenient and easy to grasp, required little effort, and appeared to harmonize beautifully with religious teachings; for whenever reason encountered doubts or wished to over-scrutinize a particular point, it was unceremoniously placed into the stocks of faith <note>original: *Stock des Glaubens*—a metaphor for forcing reason to submit to religious dogma.</note>—

Because reasonable men at that time sensed the deficiencies of common school instruction in most countries, Comenius’s teaching style caused a stir almost everywhere. From a distance, he was widely regarded in several places as the man who possessed the necessary skill to rehabilitate the crumbling school systems. Consequently, in the year 1638, he was invited to Sweden for this purpose, where he was to be commissioned to reform all schools throughout the entire kingdom. However, he declined this invitation for unknown reasons, though he did promise to assist the commission that was to be established with sound advice. Presumably, he already had his sights set on England, where he had already arranged for a Latin edition of his *Preludes to Pansophy* <note>original: *praeludiorum pansophiae*; a work that introduced his ideas to the English-speaking world and caught the attention of the circle around Samuel Hartlib.</note> to be published in 1637
