### 9. Johann Amos Comenius

...had <note>This sentence continues from the previous page, referring to Comenius's schoolbooks</note>, after they had already been printed previously in the Bohemian language at Lesna.

England certainly promised him a richer harvest than the poorer Sweden; and since the friends he had there recommended him as the most capable man for the improvement of schools, he actually received an invitation from the Parliament of that time to come to England. He arrived there in September 1641; however, since internal unrest <note>Referring to the beginning of the English Civil War (1642–1651).</note> was breaking out in this kingdom at that very time, which occupied Parliament with matters of a completely different nature, school instruction was forgotten as a result. Comenius soon saw that England was not the country where his <term>Pansophy</term> <note>From the Greek *pansophia*, meaning "universal wisdom." This was Comenius's grand project to synthesize all human knowledge into a single Christian framework.</note> would be able to flourish and bear golden fruit. That he truly had this intention is evident from his **Precursor to Universal Wisdom** <note>original: "Prodromo pansophiae"</note>, which he had printed in London in 1639 as his forerunner, and in which a subscription was proposed, without which his Pansophy would not have been able to appear. It is probable enough in itself that the internal war of that time hindered the intended improvement of the schools in England; but even this *Precursor* contained enough internal reasons to convince sensible men that Comenius’s designs were nothing more than a **pious chimera** <note>A "chimera" refers to an impossible or foolish fancy; the author is suggesting Comenius's ideas were unrealistic or outdated.</note>, which came at least a few thousand years too late.

### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

the truth of his prophecy now experienced to his own detriment; however, a visionary <note>German: *Schwärmer*; a term used historically to describe a person prone to religious enthusiasm or mystical delusions.</note> does not let himself be led astray by such things. **Charles Gustav** turned his weapons against Denmark, and **Comenius** accompanied him immediately with a similar panegyric <note>original: "Panegyrico"; a formal speech or written text of high praise.</note>.

The exiles from **Bohemia** and **Moravia** had now, through their own imprudence, deprived themselves of the generous protection they had enjoyed in **Lissa**, and nothing remained for them but to seek other refuges. They scattered and sought shelter wherever they could. **Comenius**, their bishop, traveled to **Silesia**, then to **Frankfurt an der Oder**, and because he was not safe there from the plague, to **Hamburg**, and from there to **Amsterdam**. All of this must have happened in a very short time, because **Lissa**, according to Bayle <note>original: "Baile"; likely referring to the influential scholar and biographer Pierre Bayle.</note>, was burned to the ground at the end of April 1657, yet **Comenius** published his *Didactic Works* <note>original: "Opera didactica".</note> in **Amsterdam** that same year. In **Amsterdam**, he found **Laurentius de Geer**, a son of his already deceased Swedish patron, **Ludwig de Geer**, who not only received him in a friendly manner but also supported him generously from his own fortune; for this reason, **Comenius** spent the remainder of his life in this place.

The first thing he did here was to publish his previous school and pansophic <note>Pansophy was Comenius's philosophical system, which aimed to organize all human knowledge into a single, cohesive educational framework.</note> writings under the title *Didactic Works*, and

Nevertheless, de Geer was kind-hearted enough to support him most generously; he not only provided for his upkeep but also paid the costs for most of the many works that Comenius had printed during his stay in Amsterdam. There were also other wealthy merchants who, in the hope that Comenius would teach their **spoiled little sons** Latin with less effort and loss of time, were all the more willing to spend their money. Many were indeed surprised that the superintendent and bishop of the **Bohemian and Moravian Brethren** lived so entirely apart from his flock; yet that was perhaps Comenius's least concern, provided he himself was safe and provided for.

### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

had grown. But what truly dishonored him, and made him not merely contemptible but even hateful to all those who had previously valued him as a fine educator <note>original: "Schulmann"</note>, was the decisive part he took in the absurd prophecies of Christoph Kotter, Nicolaus Drabicius, and Christina Poniatowa. He carefully collected these, translated them into English <note>original: "Lateinische" (Latin). The text refers to his work *Lux in Tenebris*.</note>, and from 1657 onward not only published them several times under the title *Light in Darkness* <note>original: *Lux in tenebris*</note>, but also most stubbornly defended them against all contradictions.

Despite the fact that these alleged prophecies not only contained the grossest nonsense but had also been repeatedly refuted by actual events—for instance, regarding Charles Gustav of Sweden, George Rakotzy of Transylvania <note>original: "Siebenbürgen"</note>, and others—Comenius nonetheless continued to regard them as divine inspirations. Following their guidance, he predicted the most significant changes himself, specifically forecasting the beginning of the Millennium <note>The "thousand-year reign" of Christ on Earth, a common belief among 17th-century millenarians.</note> for the year 1672.

What made the matter even more irresponsible and hateful was that amidst this heap of rubbish were offensive prophecies directed against the House of Austria and the Pope, whose empires were supposedly to be destroyed and eradicated by the Kings of Sweden, Cromwell, and Rakotzy. Comenius, like all fanatics <note>original: "Schwärmer"; a term used for religious enthusiasts or visionaries, often with a derogatory connotation of being detached from reality.</note> of the first order, had so little sense of the offensiveness of these assertions that he even

When a madman is guilty of such excesses, he deserves pity; but from a man who announced himself not only as a philosopher but also as a reformer of all human knowledge and institutions <note>Comenius's famous "Pansophy" aimed to organize all human knowledge into a single system.</note>, one really does not know what to think. ### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

I will say nothing further here regarding these alleged prophecies, because I intend to describe the lives of Kotter, Drabicius, Poniatowá <note>Christoph Kotter, Nicolaus Drabicius, and Christina Poniatowská were three "prophets" whose visions Comenius collected and published, believing they foretold the fall of the Habsburgs and the Papacy.</note>, and other similar fanatics separately in the following sections.

The older Comenius grew in years, the deeper he sank into religious fervor <note>original: "Schwärmerey"; a term used in the 18th century to describe excessive, often irrational religious enthusiasm or mysticism.</note>. When the Congress of Breda <note>A peace congress held in 1667 to end the Second Anglo-Dutch War.</note> was held in 1667, he sent his *Angel of Peace* <note>original: "Angelum pacis"</note> there along with the aforementioned prophecies. In this work, he recommended to the ambassadors that they should allow themselves to be guided in their negotiations by the revelations of Drabicius, Kotter, and Poniatowá. He informed them that he had drafted two more writings \*) through which God intended the dawn of the universal light of the end times to rise for the human race. He claimed he had composed these writings upon God's immediate command, and he urged the ambassadors to send this letter, along with the mentioned prophecies, to all the kings and princes of the earth. One can easily imagine what kind of effect this nonsense must have had on a gathering of enlightened statesmen.

---

\*) These two writings were titled: *Christianity Reconcilable through Christ the Reconciler* <note>original: "Christianismus reconciliabilis reconciliatore Christo"</note>, and *On the Universal Improvement of All Human Affairs* <note>original: "De omnimoda rerum humanarum emendatione"; this was Comenius's great unfinished work on the reform of human society.</note>. The first was never printed; the latter, however, was published from the manuscript by Buddeus <note>Johann Franz Buddeus (1667–1729), a prominent German Lutheran theologian.</note>, thirty years after the author's death.

### 9. Johann Amos Comenius,

additions to Balbinus's *Learned Bohemia* <note>original Latin: *Bohemia docta* by Bohuslav Balbín, a Jesuit historian known for his defense of the Czech language</note>; unless it is a case of confusion with the *Consideration of the Causes of the Bohemian War* <note>original Latin: *Consideratione causarum belli Bohemici*</note> begun in the year 1618, which Ludwig Camerarius published anonymously in 1647, in quarto format.

27. *History of the Persecutions of the Bohemian Church* <note>original Latin: *Historia Persecutionum ecclesiae Bohemicae*</note>, from the very beginnings of its conversion to Christianity up until the year 1632. Without author or place, 1648, duodecimo; which Comenius indeed did not write alone, but did partially elaborate. It is one of his most useful works, as it contains much otherwise unknown information; however, it is presented with great partiality <note>meaning it is highly biased toward his own religious group</note>, in that the Bohemian and Moravian Brethren <note>the *Unitas Fratrum*, a Protestant group that faced intense suppression during the Counter-Reformation</note> are portrayed here as purely saints and martyrs, even though one knows from other sources—and in part from Comenius’s own history—how much cause they gave for the persecutions raised against them. A Bohemian <note>Czech</note> translation by Adam Hartmann, one of the authors, appeared with Comenius’s preface in Leszno <note>original: Lissa</note>, 1655, and Amsterdam, 1663, the latter edition of which was repeated in Zittau, 1756, duodecimo. A German translation appeared under the title: *Brief Historical Concept of the Persecutions* etc. without place, but in Switzerland 1650, duodecimo, and under the title: *Bohemian Little Book of Martyrs*, Zurich, 1669, duodecimo. A better version was given by Johann Theophilus Elsner under the title: *Bohemian Martyrology* <note>original Latin: *Martyrologium Bohemicum*</note>

## 10 Giordano Bruno *),
->a bold scorner of religion.<-

Also an unfortunate man, who certainly possessed enough wit and intellect to recognize many of the prevailing prejudices of his time, but who through—

In truth, Bruno went very far in his order in the fields of mathematics and philosophy—farther than his order could tolerate, and farther than was healthy for him. He recognized the flaws of the **Aristotelian philosophy** <note>The teachings of Aristotle, which dominated medieval and Renaissance universities as the unquestioned foundation of logic and science.</note> prevailing at that time and mocked it. This alone was sufficient to draw upon him the hatred and persecution of his era, in which Aristotle still held a canonical authority. However, he did not stop there, but also contested the doctrines of religion, particularly **transubstantiation** <term>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist literally become the body and blood of Christ.</term> and the **virginity of Mary**. Scioppius <note>Caspar Schoppe, an eyewitness to Bruno's trial.</note> explicitly mentions these two articles; and although Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a pioneering historian of philosophy whose work the author is scrutinizing.</note> disputes his testimony because no attack on these two doctrines is found in Bruno's writings, this objection is mere hair-splitting. For Brucker himself admits that he had seen only very few of Bruno's writings. Furthermore, it will become clear from what follows that Bruno declared all **positive religion** <term>Religions based on specific historical revelations and established laws, rather than "natural religion" based on reason alone.</term> to be a silly fairy tale and "priestcraft" <note>original German: *Pfaffenbetrug* — a derogatory term for clerical deception or religious fraud.</note>; therefore, it is not clear why he should have spared these two specific doctrines. Since these would strike an independent philosopher more than others, it is much more probable that Bruno began doubting the truth of the Catholic religion precisely with these two doctrines.

astic life <note>Continuing from the previous page: "monastic life."</note> very soon, especially since it was ill-suited to his natural vivacity—which later even degenerated into debauchery. He thus left the monastery and his fatherland and traveled to **Geneva**. **Bayle** <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a famous French philosopher and lexicographer.</note> concludes from a letter by **Acidalius** <note>Valens Acidalius, a 16th-century German critic and poet.</note>, in which he says of **Bruno**: *he departed as an exile* <note>original Latin: "exul abiit"</note>, that he was driven out of Italy. However, others have already noted that this meaning is not contained in those specific words. Moreover, it is the custom of neither the monastic orders nor the Roman Church to banish their rebellious members; rather, they at least imprison them. It is therefore quite certain that he left Italy voluntarily.

The time when this occurred can be determined by conjecture. **Schioppius** <note>Kaspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a controversial scholar and convert to Catholicism who witnessed Bruno’s execution.</note>, who wrote his letter in February 1600, says in the same:

> who, since eighteen years ago, began to doubt <term>Transubstantiation</term> <note>The Catholic doctrine that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual body and blood of Christ.</note>—indeed, to deny it entirely—and immediately to call into question the virginity of the Blessed Mary, went to **Geneva**, and having stayed there for two years, was then cast out to **Lyon**. <note>original Latin: "qui cum jam annis abhinc octodecim de Transubstantiatione — dubitare; imo eam prorsus negare, et statim virginitatem B. Mariae — in dubium vocare coepisset, Genevam abiit, et biennium istic comoratus — inde ejectus Lugdanum."</note>

According to this, he must have left Italy in 1582, and most sources also provide this year. However, the other circumstances do not align with this. By 1584, **Bruno** was already in **London**, after having spent a considerable amount of time in **Lyon**, **Toulouse**, and **Paris**, and having previously stayed in **Geneva** for two years. He must, therefore, have left Italy as early as 1580.

# 10. Giordano Bruno, <note>original: Jordanus Brunus</note>

...fled Italy, and in the following, it will become clear that he was indisputably in Paris in 1582. Schoppe <note>original: Scioppius</note> wrote his accounts from memory, and moreover in a private letter, and thus he could easily have been mistaken.

Despite the fact that his stay in **Geneva** lasted two years, nothing about it is known. Schoppe merely says that he did not approve of the <term>Reformed religion</term> <note>A branch of Protestantism, specifically Calvinism, which was the state religion of Geneva.</note> in all its aspects, which is why he was driven out of there. **Niceron** and **Mazzuchelli** conclude from this that he had formally converted to the Reformed Church, though this does not seem to me to be implied by the words themselves. If **Bruno** had not spared the dominant religion in Italy, he would have done so even less in **Geneva**, where he believed he would have more freedom. However, tolerance was not a virtue of the **Genevans** of this century, as the examples of **Servetus** <note>Michael Servetus (1511–1553), a Spanish theologian burned at the stake in Geneva for heresy.</note> and **Simoni** <note>Simone Simoni (1532–1602), an Italian physician who fled to Geneva but was forced to leave due to religious disputes.</note> prove; the latter of whom had likewise been driven out not long before due to dissenting opinions, and **Bruno** then suffered this very same fate.

He went from **Geneva** to **Lyon**, and from there to **Toulouse**; for what purpose is not reported. It also appears that he stayed in both places for only a short time, perhaps because he did not find what he was looking for there <note>literally: "he did not find his account there," meaning he did not find it profitable or suitable</note>; for in 1582, he is already found in **Paris**, where, at first glance, better prospects opened up for him. The entire work is filled with so many ribald jokes and such low filth, as well as so many mockeries of religion, that it likely could never have been performed on a stage. The piece is dedicated to a certain **Signora Morgana**, whose morals do not appear in the best light if she was able to find pleasure in the bombastic dedication and the play as a whole. **Chaufepié** <note>Jacques George de Chaufepié (1702–1786), a biographer who updated Bayle’s dictionary.</note>, from whom I have this information, suspects that she was an Englishwoman; however, I do not see on what grounds he bases this. Since **Bruno** dedicated another writing in that very same year to the Venetian ambassador in Paris, **Giovanni Moro**, she could more likely be a person from his retinue, provided the name is not simply a fiction.

Yet **Bruno** did not only declare war on good morals, but also on the entirety of **Aristotelian philosophy**. Until then, this philosophy had been dominant in Paris, as it was at all other universities, and had attained an almost canonical authority because the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who used logic to defend religious dogma.</note> had, by necessity, harmonized it with the ruling religion. However, the **Enlightenment** <note>original: "Aufklärung"; here referring to the intellectual awakening and Humanism of the 16th century rather than the 18th-century movement.</note>, which was spreading everywhere in the 16th century, had long since made this philosophy appear suspicious. And although the university faculties and the Church still powerfully protected it for the reason mentioned above, any contradiction was welcome among others. Since it

# A Daring Mocker of Religion

Since **Bruno** lacked financial support, he was keen to cause a sensation, and to that end, he took advantage of the prevailing spirit of his time. He therefore held public lectures in which he, at the very least, did not spare the dominant philosophy. **Scioppius** <note>Caspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a German scholar and controversialist who witnessed Bruno's execution.</note> says that he was an extraordinary professor <note>original: "außerordentlicher Professor"; a faculty position often held by someone without a permanent chair.</note> in Paris because he could not become an ordinary professor, as the ordinary ones were required to attend Mass—something to which **Bruno** would not agree. **Brucker** <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), a famous historian of philosophy.</note> disputes the fact that he was an extraordinary professor, because neither **Lannoy** <note>Jean de Launoy (1603–1678), an expert on the history of the University of Paris.</note> in his *The Fortune of Aristotle in the Academy of Paris* <note>original: "de fort. Aristot. in acad Paris."</note> nor **Boulay** <note>César-Egasse Du Boulay (d. 1678), author of the history of the University of Paris.</note> in his history of the university mention anything about it. However, it seems to me that **Scioppius** only means to say that **Bruno** gave lectures without being a professor; for "extraordinary professors" in the modern sense likely did not yet exist at that time. 

Meanwhile, his attacks on **Aristotelian philosophy** during his first stay seem to have been quite modest and only incidental; at least, the writings he published in Paris at that time altogether concern the foolish whims of the **Lullian art of memory and recollection** <note>A complex mnemonic system created by Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) intended to organize all knowledge.</note>. He presumably refashioned these into more than one form out of a lack of financial support, and in doing so, he betrayed a great deal of muddled imagination and philosophical enthusiasm <note>original: "Schwärmerey"; this term suggests a wild, visionary, or fanatical devotion to ideas rather than rational thought.</note>, but all the less reason and judgment. These writings are: *On the Shadows of Ideas* <note>original: "De umbris idearum"</note> and *The Art of Memory* <note>original: "ars memoriae"</note>.

# A Bold Mocker of Religion

Despite this acclaim, Bruno did not stay long in Paris. Instead, he traveled—it seems in 1583—to London. It is unknown what prompted this change of location; Scioppius <note>Kaspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a scholar who witnessed Bruno’s execution and wrote a detailed account of his life and trial.</note> merely says, *he set out for London* <note>original: "Londinum profectus"</note>, and as far as I am aware, no further light is shed on the matter in his own writings. Presumably, through his attacks on the prevailing religion and philosophy, he saw no hope for any further promotion in Paris; therefore, he believed he might find such prospects in London. He sought a recommendation to the French ambassador there, **Michel de Castelnau**, Lord of **Mauvissière**, who received him very kindly, kept him in his house, and hosted him for nearly two years—for Bruno resided in his home from 1583 until the beginning of 1585. Here, he soon became acquainted with the witty—

> ...from that time he displayed his skill in speaking extensively on that subject, which I greatly admired—those things I once neglected in my youth because of their obscurity, I now yearned to review in my more mature years. Nor do I repent the deed—the little book by <term>GIORDANO BRUNO</term> on *A Brief Summary of Architecture and the Completion of the Art of Lully* <note>original: "de compendiosa Architectura et complemento Artis Lullii"</note>, published in Paris in 1582, at whose [terms like] *irum, ile, are* and *bonificabilities* <note>These are technical terms from the combinatorial logic of Ramon Llull and Bruno, often mocked by classical scholars for their strange-sounding linguistic inventions.</note> I had laughed; he made them so dear to me that, although they might offend those delicate followers of Cicero with the roughness of their language, they nonetheless held my interest during reading through the delight of the art itself. <term>Bünemann</term> in *Catalogue of Rare Books* p. 117, and from there <term>Clement</term> in *Curious Library* Vol. 5, p. 243. If one counts back 33 years from 1615, one arrives at the year 1582.

# 10. Giordano Bruno

Since Bruno’s wit and disposition regarding religion were entirely to the taste of these gentlemen, they very soon became intimate and held secret meetings, where philosophical subjects and mockeries of religion seem to have been the primary focus. Because people at that time still held very strict views on the latter point everywhere, such meetings had to take place in great secrecy, and their members were chosen with much caution. To what extent Queen Elizabeth knew of this is unknown; however, it is asserted that Bruno was very well known to her \*).

Such a society was the best nourishment for Bruno’s already dominant mindset, and he now began to develop his system more closely, both in philosophy and in religion; therefore, his most important writings also fall within the period of his stay in London. One of the first was *The Ash Wednesday Supper* <note>original: "la Cena de le Ceneri"</note>, which is framed as table conversations held on Ash Wednesday—that is, the first evening of spring. From this brief presentation, it is already evident that Bruno’s system in this regard corresponds entirely with the later doctrinal structure of **Spinoza** <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a philosopher famous for "Pantheism," the idea that God and the universe are one and the same.</note>.

The third work published in London, and likewise dedicated to the French ambassador, deals with *On the Infinite Universe and Worlds* <note>original: "de l'Infinito universo e Mondi"</note>. It consists of five dialogues in which he again seeks to prove, at great length, the infinity of the world and the existence of countless celestial bodies; otherwise, however, he subscribes to the opinion of **Copernicus**.

However, in order not to violate Justice—which is the foundation of all virtues—during this transplantation of virtues to the heavens, he devises a council of the gods presided over by Jupiter, where each virtue is assigned its place according to its importance and dignity. Jupiter opens the assembly with a speech in which he confesses that the gods themselves had, from ancient times, been mere figments of the imagination <note>original: "Hirngespinste"</note> with which the priests had deceived the human race; therefore, they had been rightfully driven out of heaven. 

Yet, what grieved him most was that their successors were a thousand times worse, for the ancient heroes were infinitely preferable to the modern saints, and the new superstition was far more intolerable than the old. He declares all miracles to be fables, yet maintains that pagan mythology is by no means as incomprehensible, absurd, and monstrous as Jewish and Christian theology. He wishes that men would cast off all prejudices against every **positive religion** and let themselves be guided solely by **natural religion**, which he now divides into forty-eight sections according to the number of the constellations <note>Bruno refers to the 48 Ptolemaic constellations which were the standard in 16th-century astronomy.</note> in the sky, each of which bears the name of a virtue.

By this I mean to ask: can a deity arise from the union of human nature with the nature of a horse, one worthy of being placed in the heavens? In the attached poems, he praises the beauty of English women. <note>original: "Frauenzimmer." In 18th-century German, this term was a polite collective noun for women or "the fair sex."</note>

Even though Bruno had distinguished patrons in London, his stay there was not of long duration; instead, he returned to Paris in the same aforementioned year. Scioppius <note>Caspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a scholar known for his eyewitness account of Bruno’s execution, though his biographical details are often contested.</note> and all others who have described Bruno’s life after him know only of a single stay in Paris. They confuse his history to such an extent that even Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), author of a monumental history of philosophy, who struggled to reconcile the dates of Bruno's travels.</note>, who described his life very thoroughly and with much diligence, considered the difficulties to be unsolvable. However, the matter becomes easy and clear as soon as one has no hesitation in departing from Scioppius’s report, which he wrote down merely from memory and hearsay; therefore, it cannot be held up against better records. It is undeniable that Bruno was in Paris in 1582 and partly still in 1583; it is equally undeniable that he was there in 1585 and 1586, and just as undeniable that he lived in the house of Lord Castelnau <note>Michel de Castelnau, Sieur de la Mauvissière, the French ambassador to England who provided Bruno with a home and intellectual sanctuary.</note> in London in 1584 and part of 1585, who supported him for nearly two years. The chronology of his history thus resolves itself.

### 10. Giordano Bruno,

It is difficult to understand why Bruno left a place so soon where he seemingly fared so well. Perhaps his natural restlessness and inclination for change did not allow him to remain long in one place. For the claim made by La Croze <note>Mathurin Veyssière de La Croze (1661–1739), a French scholar and librarian who wrote about Bruno</note> that he was expelled from Wittenberg is completely unfounded, as on March 8, 1588, he delivered a public farewell speech which, by his own account, was attended not only by students but also by the academic senate, the professors, and the doctors. This speech, which exists in print, is an adventurous mishmash of insults directed at the Roman Church, praises for Luther and the Protestants, mythology, and flights of imagination, and it seems to have been composed entirely in the spirit of the Lullian art <note>The "Art of Ramon Llull," a complex system of logic and mnemonics using revolving circles to categorize all knowledge</note>. In it, he once again praises the kindnesses shown to him in Wittenberg, but mentions his departure and the motives for it only with the few words <note>original: "cum de abscessu cogitarem"</note> "when I thought of my departure." On the title page, he calls himself a Doctor, and—

> —to you <note>original: "vobis"</note> [philosophy] was not only approved just now, but has been accepted for many centuries and almost everywhere in the world. You did not (unlike the custom of one or another place) turn up your noses; you did not sharpen your mockery; your cheeks were not puffed with anger; the pulpits did not thunder; no scholastic fury <note>original: "scholasticus furor," referring to the aggressive academic debates and persecution common in the era</note> was incited against me. Instead, according to the brilliance of your humanity and learning, you conducted the matter in such a way that you appeared wise on behalf of yourselves, on behalf of others, on behalf of me, and on behalf of everyone, etc.

# A Daring Scoffer of Religion.

One might reasonably ask where he became a Doctor. However, he presumably conferred the title upon himself, as in the dedication of his *Explanation of the Thirty Seals* <note>original: "Explicationis XXX Sigillorum"</note>, which I shall mention among his writings, he calls himself a <term>doctor of a more labored theology and professor of a purer and harmless wisdom</term> <note>original: "magis laboratae theologiae doctorem, purioris et innocuae sapientiae professorem"</note>. This likely signifies nothing other than a Doctor and Professor of natural religion <note>In the 18th century, "natural religion" referred to a belief system based on reason and nature rather than divine revelation or church dogma</note>.

Scioppius <note>Gaspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a German scholar famous for his polemics and for being an eyewitness to Bruno's execution</note> expressly asserts that Bruno went from Wittenberg to Prague and published various wicked and dangerous books there. Brucker <note>Johann Jakob Brucker (1696–1770), an influential historian of philosophy</note> attacks him very harshly for this, considering it quite improbable that Bruno would have ventured into a Catholic university, and deems it a very poor conclusion to assume he was in Prague simply because some of his works were printed there. However, Brucker’s own argument works against him; for if Prague had been as strictly Catholic at that time as he imagines, Bruno’s writings could not have been printed there either. Scioppius is only mistaken in stating that certain works were printed in Prague which actually appeared later in Frankfurt. Regardless, Bruno truly did travel from Wittenberg to Prague, as is evident not only from the place of publication of some of his writings but also from the dedication of one of them, *On the Scrutiny of Species and the Combinatory Lamp of Lull* <note>original: "de specierum scrutinio et Lampade combinatoria Lullii"</note>, which he [dedicated] to the Spa—

### 10. Giordano Bruno,

...dedicated to the Spanish envoy to Emperor Rudolf II <note>Rudolf II (1552–1612) was known for his patronage of the occult and sciences in Prague</note>, Wilhelm de S. Brucker also failed to consider that this city and its university were not nearly as Catholic then as they became after the Battle of White Mountain <note>A decisive 1620 battle that led to the forced re-Catholicization of Bohemia; before this, the region was a stronghold for various Protestant groups</note>. On the contrary, the Protestants, or so-called Hussites <note>Followers of the reformer Jan Hus, who predated Martin Luther</note>, held great power in both the city and the university; thus, Bruno was, to all appearances, completely safe there.

He undoubtedly believed he could find success at the university here by lecturing on the <term>Lullian Art</term> <note>A complex system of logic and mnemonics developed by the 13th-century mystic Ramon Llull, which Bruno adapted into his own memory systems</note> and his eclectic philosophy. Indeed, besides the aforementioned work—in which he merely repeated his previously published Lullian whims—he also had his *One Hundred and Sixty Articles against the Mathematicians and Philosophers of this Time* <note>original: "Articulos CLX adversus hujus tempestatis Mathematicos atque philosophos"</note> printed there. However, he either found his hopes frustrated, or he failed to find the necessary security even here. Regardless, his stay in Prague was not of long duration, and he must have departed from there either later that same year or at the beginning of the following one.

# 10. Giordano Bruno,

...explains in the dedication of one of his most distinguished works.

The second work, *On the Triple Minimum and Measure, according to the principles of the three speculative sciences and many active arts* <note>original: "de triplici Minimo et mensura ad trium speculativarum scientiarum et multarum activarum artium principia"</note>, encompasses at once geometrical, physical, and metaphysical content. This alone makes the work obscure and causes the author's true meaning to waver countless times—especially since it is actually written in hexameters <note>A form of poetic meter traditionally used for epic poetry, like the works of Homer or Virgil; Bruno used it here for a technical philosophical treatise</note>, although a prose explanation has been added. Like most of his other writings, it is a strange mixture of the good and the bad, the true and the false, the latter of which always stems from the author's extravagant imagination. This is already evident from the fact that he was able to treat such abstract matters in hexameters.

In the application of his geometrical teachings *on the minimum* <note>original: "de minimo"</note>, many remarkable things appear, especially the doctrine of **Monads** <term>Monads: From the Greek word for 'unit,' these are fundamental, indivisible building blocks of reality. While often associated with Leibniz, Bruno used them to describe the intersection of mathematics, physics, and metaphysics</term>. Among the moderns, he was presumably the first to bring this theory back into play, which **Leibniz** <note>Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716), a celebrated German philosopher and mathematician who is most famous for his own "Monadology"</note> later refined; consequently, **la Croze** <note>Maturin Veyssière La Croze (1661–1739), a French scholar and librarian who noted the similarities between Bruno's and Leibniz's systems</note> later publicly accused the latter of having borrowed the idea from Bruno. His "Minimum is the substance of things. It is, I say, the matter or element, the efficient cause and the whole: the point in the magnitude of dimensions, the atom in bodies, the monad in numbers" <note>original: "Minimum est substantia rerum. Est inquam, materia seu elementum, efficiens et totum: punctum in magnitudine dimensionum, atomus in corporibus, monas in numeris"</note>—is thus the true Leibnizian Monad. But now, observe what application this has to the human soul. The **architect-spirit** <note>original: "Spiritus architectus"</note>, as

It actually consists of two works: **On the Monad, Number, and Figure**, and **On the Innumerable, the Immense, and the Unfigurable.** In the first, he deals in eleven chapters with the mysteries of the numbers 1 to 10 and their geometric figures; for each number, he cites everything known to him about it. For the number six, for example, he notes that God created the world in six days and that the throne of Solomon <note>The biblical king famous for his wisdom; his throne with six steps (1 Kings 10:19) was often interpreted symbolically in mystical traditions.</note> had six steps. At the same time, the meanings of the numbers according to the opinion of the ancient Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, who believed that numbers were the fundamental essence of all things and held mystical significance.</note> are provided.

### 10. Giordano Bruno,

...the aim of this whole undertaking is, because he believed that nature gives to every thing its number and figure, from which its properties could simultaneously be recognized; on which occasion much that is useless and excessive is said regarding the secret power of numbers. Occasionally, all sorts of claims occur which partly contradict his previously expressed opinions, for example, regarding the reality of the devil and the idea that sorcerers could banish and compel him to reveal hidden and future things; furthermore, the reliability of palmistry <term>Palmistry: Also known as chiromancy, the practice of fortune-telling through the study of the palm.</term>, which he seeks to prove from Job 13:14: *I carry my soul in my hands.* <note>original Latin: "animam meam porto in manibus meis." Following this, he was publicly degraded <note>The ceremonial "un-priesting" or stripping of clerical status, which involved removing vestments and scraping the fingertips that had been anointed with holy oil.</note>, from which it is clear that he must have been a priest in his former Order; he was then excommunicated and handed over to the secular authorities in the customary manner <note>The Church used the legal fiction of "handing over to the secular arm" to avoid the direct shedding of blood, while fully expecting the state to carry out the death penalty.</note>. Bruno appeared composed during this scene and, after its conclusion, replied only that his judges perhaps felt more fear in pronouncing the sentence than he did in hearing it. The Governor of Rome, to whom he had now been handed over, delayed the execution of the sentence for another eight days to give the unfortunate man time to prevent it through a recantation; however, Bruno remained unmoved and was therefore led to the pyre on February 17 and burned alive.

### 10. Giordano Bruno.

...d. In his final moments, a crucifix was held before him; however, he pushed it away with a grim expression. Various writers, who date his execution to February 9th, confuse the day of sentencing with the day of execution. Scioppius's <note>Gaspar Schoppe (1576–1649), a German scholar and convert to Catholicism who was an eyewitness to Bruno's execution.</note> letter is dated the 17th, and in it, he states explicitly: "Today, therefore, he was led to the stake or the pyre." <note>original Latin: "hodie igitur ad rogum sive pyram deductus est"</note> *).

I do not understand how people in recent times can still argue over the question of why he was burned in Rome. Heumann <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a prominent German philosopher and historian of logic.</note> claims it was because he was a Lutheran, and goes to great and useless trouble in his *Philosophical Acts* <note>original Latin title: *Actis philosophicis*</note> to portray him as a martyr for evangelical truth;

> *) Bayle <note>Pierre Bayle (1647–1706), a French philosopher known for his influential *Historical and Critical Dictionary*.</note>, who likewise gives the date as February 9th, takes his skepticism a bit too far when he considers it still uncertain whether Bruno was actually burned, following which others have speculated that he was only burned in effigy <note>The practice of burning a statue or portrait of a person when the person themselves could not be executed.</note>. However, I do not see for what reason one would want to cast doubt on the testimony of Scioppius, who was present in Rome at that very time. Although Scioppius has been accused of several other inaccuracies in his account of Bruno, these could at most have occurred because he had them only through hearsay, without detracting from what he saw with his own eyes. Moreover, upon a closer investigation of Bruno's life, I have found that people have been a little too generous with accusations of falsehood against Scioppius; for his account is very true and correct in almost every detail.

### 10. Giordano Bruno,

...pushed, but also everything that was most sacred—not only to the Roman Church but also to every **positive religion** <note>In this context, "positive religion" refers to religions based on historical revelation and established laws, such as Christianity or Judaism, as opposed to "natural religion" based on reason alone.</note>, and even to the Protestant faith—such as the doctrine of the **Trinity**, of **Christ** and his **two natures**, was most bitterly mocked and derided. It appears that his **Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast** <note>original title: *Spaccio della Bestia trionfante* (1584), a dialogue where Bruno uses astronomical allegories to satirize religious and moral corruption.</note> was known to his judges; and this reckless book had already deprived him of all safety in all Protestant countries. A single allegory from it was sufficient to bring him to the stake in Rome. Had **Heumann** <note>Christoph August Heumann (1681–1764), a German literary historian who argued Bruno was a crypto-Protestant.</note> known this book, he would surely have been careful not to portray its author as a martyr for Protestant doctrine, especially since it cannot even be proven that **Bruno** ever publicly professed his faith in any of the Protestant churches.

is—and has always been—a trick used by ignorant and angry defenders of every dominant religion: to brand anyone who finds it necessary to deviate from the common concepts of the Supreme Being with the name of an **atheist** <note>original: *Gottesläugner*, literally "God-denier."</note>. However, an enlightened seeker of truth should at least try to attach more precision to his expressions. **Bruno** was indeed a despiser of all **positive religion** <note>A "positive religion" is one based on specific historical revelations and established institutions, like Catholicism or Lutheranism, rather than on natural reason alone.</note>, a true **naturalist**, and a **deist**, but nothing more than that. 

What he considered to be the Supreme Being was, of course, not formulated in the way the Roman and Protestant churches desired; it was **Nature**, or the **world-soul** <note>original: *Weltseele*. This is the idea that a spiritual essence infuses all living things and the entire universe.</note>. In his view, this being was inseparably linked to the physical world and could not be conceived without it; but it was nonetheless a supreme, infinite being; it was still a God, and consequently, **Bruno** was anything but an atheist. Even if a third party believes they can prove through a series of logical deductions (and what cannot be "proven" that way?) that such a system carries contradictions and thus ultimately leads to atheism, the defender of such a system still cannot be treated as an avowed atheist, because he either does not see these conclusions or does not admit to them. Therefore, let us say no more of this accusation.

### 10. Giordano Bruno.

...[human] origin of all **positive religions** <note>A "positive religion" is one based on specific historical revelations and established institutions, like Catholicism or Lutheranism, rather than on natural reason alone.</note> was true and sincere, and he felt bound for that reason to seal his conviction with death, thus becoming a martyr for a truth he believed in. I, for my part, do not see what could move a rational man to become a martyr for a truth that is not only useless, but even harmful and dangerous. Civilized human society across God's entire earth is now so closely intertwined with one positive religion or another that such a sudden overthrow of them, as **Bruno** desired and attempted, must inevitably result in the collapse of all social happiness. Even assuming that **naturalism** <note>The philosophical view that everything arises from natural properties and causes, and supernatural or spiritual explanations are excluded.</note> is truth, it is a truth that takes everything away from the sensory-driven human being and gives him nothing in return. That **Bruno** did not see this was shortsightedness; but that for the sake of such a truth he made himself an object of hatred throughout his entire life, let himself be driven poor and needy from one city to another, from one country to another, and finally even allowed himself to be placed upon the **pyre** <note>original: *Scheiterhaufen*. Bruno was famously burned at the stake in Rome in 1600.</note>, could surely be nothing other than the extreme degree of **madness** <note>original: *Wahnwitz*.</note>. There are more people in our day who think similarly to **Bruno** regarding religion than there were in his own time; however, I highly doubt that many among them would be inclined to follow him in this regard.

I believe that from what has been said of his life so far, the character of the man can be fairly well determined. He possessed, when he wished, an extraordinary amount of wit; for his *The Expulsion of the Triumphant Beast* <note>original: *Spaccio della Bestia trionfante*, a satirical dialogue published by Bruno in 1584 that critiques contemporary morality and religion.</note> is—setting aside the morality and several shallow and distorted allegories—a true masterpiece of wit, provided that Sidney <note>Sir Philip Sidney (1554–1586), the English poet and courtier who was a friend and patron to Bruno in London.</note> and others did not assist him with it. 

But his **imagination** was even greater, and this constitutes the dominant trait in his character; at least, it peers out everywhere that calm reason should have reflected and examined. However, it is not an imagination refined by taste or guided by the power of judgment, but rather a rampaging, unrestrained one that sweeps everything along in its vortex. His farewell speech at **Wittenberg** <note>delivered in 1588 as Bruno departed the University of Wittenberg; it was notable for its high praise of Martin Luther, despite Bruno's own unorthodox views.</note> is a true masterpiece of a seething fantasy which, in its delirium, storms together everything from all parts of the world, whether it be good or bad, relevant to the subject or not.

Bruno wrote several Latin poems in this style, such as *De immenso et innumerabilibus*, to express his cosmological theories.</note>, where one finds little true poetic beauty but all the more fanatical turbulence, which molds language and ideas according to its own whim. Hence also the lack of connection between his opinions and the incessant contradiction in which he stands with himself. ing is remarkable among other reasons because it clearly shows the progression from a physical illness to fanaticism <note>German: *Schwärmerey*. As noted previously, this refers to a state of religious delusion or excessive emotional enthusiasm.</note>, and from there to the grossest deception.

Elisabeth Barton, or as she is also called Berton, a notorious English fanatic and prophetess of the 16th century, was of humble origin, first becoming known in 1525 as a maidservant to a certain Thomas Knob of Aldington in Kent. Since she was hysterical to a high degree, and was therefore seized by frequent bouts of anxiety, so-called "suffocation of the womb," <term>suffocation of the womb: *Ausstoßen der Mutter*. An archaic medical term for hysteria, where it was believed the uterus moved upward in the body, causing a choking sensation or "globus hystericus."</term> fainting fits, and delusions of the mind accompanied by violent distortions of her limbs and unusual convulsions, it was not surprising in such a superstitious century that the common people—who remain like children in their knowledge of nature and its forces—believed they saw something extraordinary in her. The public always regards such a sick person as either possessed or as a saint, and it depends merely on the circumstances, and often on the caprice of the "guardians of the people," <note>Referring to religious or political leaders who guide public opinion.</note> which of these two qualities shall be attributed to her. Some insignificant and wavering utterances, which happened to come true by chance, caused her to be viewed as a prophetess; and when she noticed the inclination of the people toward this prejudice, she was clever enough to use it to her advantage, and perhaps fanaticism—

Since the prestige of the Roman Church was also beginning to waver in England at this time, the priest of Aldington (named Masters) considered this person a skillful tool to strengthen the old belief in miracles of his church, to make his chapel famous in the neighborhood, and to enrich himself in the process. Until now, the inspirations of Elizabeth Barton were intended only to benefit a few churches and monasteries; however, around 1532, it was deemed appropriate to have her play a more significant role. which his teachers therefore lavished on him, made him quite naturally proud and puffed up. He believed himself alone to be enough, believed he could derive all knowledge from the own fullness of his genius <note>In the 18th-century sense, "Genie" refers to innate, often restless, intellectual talent</note>, and soon learned to despise everything that did not originate from it. At that time, here as elsewhere, the well-known and vexatious disputes between the so-called Orthodox and Pietists <note>The "Orthodox" were traditional Lutherans, while "Pietists" emphasized personal devotion and internal experience over rigid dogma</note> had broken out. ### 12. Johann Conrad Dippel,

perhaps he believed he could make himself popular here through his vigorous zeal against the **Pietists** <term>Pietists: Followers of a reform movement within Lutheranism that emphasized individual piety and "living faith" over strict adherence to institutional dogma</term>; however, he was short-sighted enough not to see that his peculiar opinions—and especially the proposition he defended in Giessen—must have been more hated in Wittenberg than Pietism itself. The outcome also proved this sufficiently. He had been recommended to the Doctor and Professor of Theology **Hanneken**; yet the manner in which Hanneken received him soon convinced him that Wittenberg would be no fertile ground for his peculiar genius.

Dippel was still set on his "errant knight-errantry" <note>original: "irrende Ritterschaft"—a metaphor for his combative, wandering lifestyle as a self-appointed champion</note> against the Pietists, and when he heard that they were little esteemed in **Strasburg**, he immediately imagined that this was the place where he could earn both bread and honor. However, upon his arrival, he found the situation quite different. **Spener** <note>Philipp Jakob Spener (1635–1705), the influential founder of Pietism</note> had many secret friends there, and in general, the local Protestant theologians were very careful and cautious not to reveal any vulnerability to the dominant **Catholic religion**; consequently, no one here wanted to concern themselves with his aforementioned polemical writing against the Pietists. Yet his genius was fertile enough to open new prospects for him. Since he could not show himself as an **orthodox brawler** <note>original: "orthodoxen Klopffechter"—a term for those who engaged in aggressive, prize-fighter-like academic debates over doctrine</note>, he wanted at least to shine as a deep-thinking philosopher; and since he completely lacked true philosophy and thorough scholarship, he sought only to cause a sensation through his eccentricity—

Nothing came of the laboring <note>original: "laboriren," referring to experimental work in an alchemical laboratory</note>; but so as not to come away entirely empty-handed, he knew how to extract from the gullibility of others the profit that his art could not provide. Since Dippel could not prove any of his assertions, he was declared in September 1719 to be a slanderer of honest men and a disturber of the public peace, losing his title of honor. He was placed in shackles and very soon transported to **Bornholm**, where his confinement was initially narrow and harsh. However, because he knew how to chatter about all sorts of things and occupied himself with healing <note>original: "Curiren"</note>, he soon obtained greater freedom through the indulgence of the governor. He was permitted to receive visitors, listen to the sick, prescribe remedies for them, and engage in laboratory work <term>laboriren: conducting chemical or alchemical experiments, a common pursuit for Dippel</term>. Yet the spirit of contradiction was not stifled by his imprisonment. Some crude, ancient figures of gold had been found on the island of **Bornholm**, which **Jacob von Melle** <note>a Lübeck-based historian and theologian known for his work on northern antiquities</note> considered in a specific treatise to be the national idols of the ancient Norse peoples; however, Dippel saw fit to declare them Egyptian, despite knowing very little about antiquities. His treatise against **von Melle** was printed in **Hamburg** in 1725.

### 11. Johann Conrad Dippel,

Dippel was able to live quietly on the island of **Bornholm** because he received his necessary provisions from the court and was protected from his most dangerous enemy: his own tempestuous passions. However, after a confinement of nearly seven years, he was released from his prison in June 1725 through the intercession of the Queen of Denmark and set at liberty once more. He intended to travel by ship to **Stralsund** and on to **Germany**; however, as there was no opportunity to do so, he had himself ferried to **Cimbrishafen** <note>modern Simrishamn</note> in **Schonen** <note>Scania, the southernmost province of Sweden</note>, and from there he traveled to **Jöstadt** <note>likely Ystad</note>. Dippel had made a name for himself through his slanders against the dominant religion, through his gold-making <note>alchemy</note>, through his **animal oil** <term>Dippel's Oil: a nitrogenous byproduct of the destructive distillation of animal bones, used medicinally and as a pest repellent</term>, and through his empirical cures. This reputation was sufficient to recommend him to the short-sighted as a man of superior insight. King **Frederick of Sweden** was afflicted with an ailment from which his physicians could not deliver him, and several of his courtiers recommended Dippel to him as a famous doctor, especially since he was already residing on Swedish soil. ## 12. Johann Conrad Dippel,

Böhme <note>Jacob Böhme (1575–1624), a German mystic and Lutheran theosophist who significantly influenced radical Pietism</note>, Gichtel <note>Johann Georg Gichtel (1638–1710), a mystic who spread Böhme's teachings and founded the "Angelic Brothers"</note>, von Helmont <note>Likely Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont, a Flemish philosopher and alchemist known for his kabbalistic and theosophical interests</note>, and other fanatics <note>original: *Schwärmer*; an 18th-century pejorative for those claiming direct divine inspiration</note> of this sort are his great guides here. According to him, God is an eternal, infinite being, who is most intimately connected with a light- and fire-matter as his body. All created spirits are ideas of God, which he brought forth in a manner similar to natural procreation, and provided them with that eternal light- and fire-matter in which lies the seed to the entire physical world. From this seed, all spirits have developed the bodies that they simultaneously animate. The spirits are either free, like the angels and the spirit of man, or unfree, like the animators of all other bodies. Spirits can act upon one another; therefore, not only angels but also devils have influence over all things. Even the human spirit possesses this faculty. Besides the higher spirit, man also has a lower sensory soul, which has its own requirements—namely, the desires—the satisfaction of which is no sin, and so forth.

I have already mentioned his most prominent writings in the preceding section; there are about seventy of them in total. However, I simply cannot bring myself to transcribe their often long and incomprehensible titles, especially since the vast majority of them are polemical writings <term>Streitschriften: aggressive pamphlets or essays written to argue against theological or political opponents</term>, which present a perpetual monotony under a hundred different guises.

<summary>This page outlines Dippel's mystical cosmology, describing God as a being of light-matter and the world as populated by "free" and "unfree" spirits. The author also expresses his exhaustion with Dippel's repetitive and voluminous polemical works.</summary>

<keywords>Johann Conrad Dippel, Jacob Böhme, Johann Georg Gichtel, Van Helmont, cosmology, light-matter, fire-matter, spirits, sensory soul, polemical writings</keywords>

repeat. Those, however, who are interested in them can find them collected in Mr. Strieder’s <term>History of Hessian Scholars</term> <note>original: *Hess. Gel. Gesch.*, referring to Friedrich Wilhelm Strieder’s *Grundlage zu einer Hessischen Gelehrten- und Schriftstellergeschichte*, a foundational biographical dictionary</note>, Volume 3, pages 112–135. I will only note that they were printed together twice under the title: <term>Opened Path to Peace with God and All Creatures</term> <note>original: *Eröffneter Weg zum Frieden mit Gott und allen Creaturen*</note>; the first time during his lifetime in Amsterdam, 1709, in <term>octavo</term> <note>original: *8*, a book size where the paper sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>, containing as many as had been published up to that point; and the second time at Berleburg, 1747, in three volumes in <term>quarto</term> <note>original: *4*, a book size where the paper sheet is folded into four leaves</note>. This edition was overseen by a certain Canz—a brother of the superior Tübingen philosopher of that name <note>likely referring to Israel Gottlieb Canz (1690–1753), a prominent philosopher and theologian; his brother oversaw this edition of Dippel's work</note>—and it is preceded by a portrait of Dippel, which is said, however, to bear no resemblance to him.
